AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL  MEMOIRS  OF  JAMES  II 29

conviction,  which  communicates  itself  to  the  reader.  It  is  as  if  one
were  listening  to  a  venerable  gentleman  narrating  the  events  of  his
life  in  a  circle  of  friends.  Clarendon's  language  is  at  once  intelligible
and  forcible.  In  it  one  recognises  a  man  who  was  at  home  with  the
classics,  and  who  found  food  for  his  soul  in  the  Book  of  books.

The  effect  which  an  historical  work  can  have  is  perhaps  nowhere
seen  more  strongly  than  in  the  History  of  the  Rebellion.  The  view
of  the  event  in  England  itself  and  in  the  educated  world  generally
has  been,  as  noticed  above,  determined  by  the  book.  The  best
authors  have  repeated  it ;  and  even  those  who  combat  it  do  not  get
beyond  the  point  of  view  given  by  him  ;  they  refute  him  in  details,  but
leave  his  view  in  the  main  unshaken.  Clarendon  belongs  to  those
who  have  essentially  fixed  the  circle  of  ideas  for  the  English  nation.

II.

ON THE AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL  MEMOIRS  OF KING  JAMES II

OF ENGLAND.

In  the  whole  range  of  modern  history  there  is  no  event  which  has
attracted  more  attention,  or  has  been  more  studied  and  described
than  the  Revolution  of  1688.  For  from  it  is  derived  the  present
condition  of  England,  and  the  opposition  between  two  great  parties,
which  sprang  up  at  that  time,  and  have  since  then  held  power
alternately :  their  controversy  keeps  alive  the  memory  of  these  events.
Moreover,  the  great  contest  of  universal  history — between  a  monarchy
acting  in  full  autonomy  and  a  parliamentary  constitution  limiting  its
action — was  in  this  case  likewise  brought  to  a  decision,  which  has
influenced  subsequent  events  even  on  the  continent.  After  absolute
power  and  republicanism,  agreeing  perhaps  in  substance,  but  in  form
totally  opposed,  have  struggled  fiercely  with  one  another,  the  world
has  in  general  come  back  to  a  mixed  constitution,  of  which  England
gave  the  first  example.  The  form  of  government  which  there  was
the  result  of  a  thousand  contests  appears  to  be  well-nigh  a  pattern  for
all  nations.

This  general  tendency  is  one  cause  of  the  immense  success  which
Macaulay's  History,  appearing  just  at  the  right  moment,  had  in
Europe.  Up  to  that  time  the  Tory  view,  as  represented  by  Hume,
had  not  yet  been  driven  from  the  field.  Macaulay  decided  the
victory  of  the  Whig  view.

One  might  conceive  the  idea  of  undertaking  a  history  of  the  views
and  descriptions  of  this  period,  which  various  and  great  intellects  have

3o  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL  MEMOIRS

attempted :  but  it  is  more  to  our  purpose  to  study  and  criticise  the
authentic  documents,  which  are  extant  from  the  period  itself.

One  of  the  first  which  presents  itself  is  a  memoir  ascribed  to  the
deposed  King,  James  IL  The  tradition  is  that  this  Prince,  like
Louis  XIV,  occupied  himself  much  with  writing  accounts  of  the
remarkable  events  of  his  life ;  and  that  at  the  critical  moment,  when
he  determined  to  leave  London,  he  found  means  of  saving  his  papers.
He  flung  them,  it  is  said,  into  a  box,  which  he  entrusted  to  the  Tuscan
ambassador;  the  latter  sent  them  first  to  Leghorn,  but  after  the
expelled  King  had  taken  up  his  abode  at  St.  Germain,  they  were  sent
back  to  him  at  that  place.  Here  he  added  some  further  notes  upon
later  events,  and  then  deposited  them  in  the  Scottish  College  at  Paris,
an  institution  founded  in  another  age  by  Cardinal  Beatoun  for  the
education  of  Scottish  missionary  students,  but  which  did  not  become  of
real  use  until  1672  under  Robert  Barclay.  The  existence  of  these  papers
was  known,  and  I  shall  presently  show  that  they  have  by  no  means
remained  undisturbed  or  unused.  But  so  far  as  one  knows,  they  were
destroyed  in  the  storms  of  the  French  Revolution.  They  were  brought
to  St.  Omer  that  they  might  be  rescued  by  being  carried  over  to
England;  but  before  that  could  be  done  they  are  said  to  have
been  concealed,  buried,  and  finally  burnt,  out  of  fear  of  the  revolu-
tionary government;  for  the  cover  bore  the  arms  of  England,  and
France  was  then  at  war  with  England.  I  repeat  this,  as  it  is  told
and  still  believed,  without  wishing  exactly  to  confirm  it.

But  if  the  autograph  notes  of  James  II  were  lost,  all  the  greater
attention  was  excited  when  it  was  understood  that  a  detailed  biography
compiled  from  them  was  in  existence.  The  first  Pretender  had
caused  it  to  be  written  soon  after  the  death  of  his  father.  The  order
is  in  existence,  in  which  he  commands  a  partial  transmission  to  St.
Germains  of  the  original  papers,  probably  for  this  purpose.  But  there
exists  no  evidence  for  the  supposition  that  Innes,  the  principal  of  the
Scotch  College  at  the  time,  had  the  largest  share  in  the  composition :
various  names  have  been  mentioned.  Enough,  that  a  detailed  work
in  four  volumes  was  compiled  on  the  life  of  James  II ;  the  Chevalier
de  St.  George  read  it,  underlined  several  passages,  and  bequeathed  it
to  his  family.  After  the  death  of  the  wife  of  the  last  Pretender,  the
Duchess  of  Albany,  it  came  into  the  hands  of  the  English  Benedictines
in  Rome,  and  was  then  purchased  by  the  English  government.  For
some  time  past,  in  fact,  chiefly  in  consequence  of  a  statement  of  Lord
Hardwicke"s,  attention  had  been  directed  to  this  monument  of  Stuart
times.  The  war  then  raging  put  many  difficulties  in  the  way  of  the
transport  of  the  manuscript.  It  was  brought  first  to  Leghorn,  then  to
Tunis,  then  to  Malta,  and  at  last  in  1 810  to  England. The  Prince

OF  KING  JAMES  II  OF  ENGLAND.  3  1

Regent,  who  had  a  certain  affection  for  the  Stuarts,  caused  it  to  be
edited  by  his  chaplain  and  librarian,  Stanier- Clarke.  In  the  year  18 16
it  appeared  in  two  handsome  volumes.

Since  then  much  use  has  been  made  of  these  volumes,  for  the  most
part  under  the  supposition  that  in  them  James  II's  account  of  the
events  of  his  own  life  is  preserved;  Guizot  has  included  them  in  his
collection  as  memoirs  of  James  II.

The  work  is  in  four  parts.  The  first  goes  down  to  the  Restoration
1660,  the  second  to  the  accession  of  James  II,  the  third  to  his
flight  from  England  at  the  end  of  1688,  the  fourth  embraces  the
rest  of  his  life.

The  first  is  not  of  great  importance,  inasmuch  as  the  main  con-
tents were  known  long  before.  It  includes  the  part  taken  by  the
Duke  in  the  Spanish-French  war  between  1650  and  1660,  in  which
he  fought  partly  under  Turenne,  partly  against  him.  In  order  to
honour  this  friend  of  his,  and  at  the  pressing  wish  of  Cardinal
Bouillon,  James  had  his  account  of  this  translated  from  the  English
original  and  gave  it  to  him,  only  on  the  condition  that  it  should
not  be  printed  in  his  (the  King's)  lifetime.  The  translation  was
printed  later  in  Ramsey's  Life  of  Turenne,  with  a  certificate  from
the  Scottish  College,  that  its  contents  were  similar  to  the  original.
It  is  composed  from  the  original  notes,  revised  and  improved  by  the
King,  and  reads  like  an  original  work.

If  I  might  venture  to  make  a  remark  on  the  mutual  relation
of  the  two  texts,  I  should  say,  that  the  French  may  sometimes
be  of  service  in  correcting  the  English  as  now  extant.

It  is  stated  in  the  French  text,  that  the  Duke  wished  to  learn
the  art  of  war  as  a  volunteer  in  the  French  army,  in  order  to  be
able  one  day  to  serve  his  brother,  the  King  of  England ;  '  ayant
une  extreme  passion  de  se  rendre  capable,  de  servir  un  jour  le  roi
son  frere.'  In  the  English  manuscript,  used  in  printing,  the  cor-
responding words  had  slipped  out.  The  editor  remarks  the  gap
and  thinks  he  can  fill  it  up  with  the  words,  he  determined  '  to  serve  for
that  he  might  be  fit  one  day  to  command ; '  and  this  mode  of
supplying  the  deficiency  has  thence  passed  into  Guizot's  translation.
But  this  confusion  introduces  an  incorrect  element  into  the  idea :
it  is  not  that  the  Duke  thought  of  being  in  command  himself,  but
of  being  in  his  brother's  service,  to  which  he  wished  one  day  to
devote  himself,  and  which  was  in  fact  his  object,  when  these  reports
were  written ;  for  according  to  the  title-page  of  the  first  book  they
were  written  long  before  the  King  ascended  the  throne.  Here,
however,  another  remark  may  be  made.  In  both  texts  the  granting
of  the  request to  enter  into  the  King's  service  is  ascribed  to  the

32  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL  MEMOIRS

favour  which  it  found  with  the  Chevalier  Barclai.  But  from  Clarendon's
State-papers  it  appears  that  it  was  maturely  considered  in  the  council
of  the  exiled  King  and  was  granted  at  the  proposal  of  Clarendon
himself.

In  the  English  original  this  is  preceded  by  another  story,  which
does  not  agree  with  Clarendon's  report.  The  Duke  relates  that
his  union  with  the  young  Duchess  of  Longueville,  which  was  on
the  tapis,  was  rejected  by  the  French  court.  Clarendon  mentions
the  affair  in  his  History:  according  to  him  it  was  rejected  by
Charles  II,  and  that  because  the  French  court  was  intending,  in
connexion  with  this  union,  to  bring  about  a  marriage  between  the
King  and  the  daughter  of  the  Duke  of  Orleans.  At  the  court
of  the  exiled  King  so  close  an  alliance  was  not  thought  advisable.

These  are  trifling  discrepancies,  but  they  involve  particulars  of
some  importance. I  will  mention  yet  another.

We  know  that  King  Charles  II,  immediately  before  the  Restora-
tion, was  hard  pressed  by  the  Spaniards,  who  wished  to  drive  him
into  concluding  a  disadvantageous  treaty;  only  by 'a  kind  of  flight
did  he  withdraw  himself  from  them.  In  the  life  of  James  II  it
is  said  on  the  other  hand,  that  the  Spaniards  were  of  opinion,  that
Charles  II  was  still  far  from  his  restoration,  and  that  only  for  this
reason  had  they  allowed  him  to  go  to  Holland.  There  can  be
no  doubt  which  of  these  two  accounts  deserves  the  most  credit.

It  is  clear  that  the  Duke  of  York  was  only  imperfectly  informed
as  to  what  went  on  in  his  brother's  cabinet.  Or  is  the  defect  to
be  ascribed  to  the  secretary  ?

But  I  will  not  linger  over  -this  portion  of  the  work.  Its  value
lies  in  the  detailed  narrative  of  the  events  of  the  war,  a  narrative
which  must  be  based  upon  a  journal  kept  during  the  campaign,  so
minute  is  it ; — but  for  the  history  of  England  it  has  no  special  value.
The  second  and  third  parts,  on  the  other  hand,  deal  almost  exclusively
with  that  history.  It  is  of  great  interest  to  notice,  how  the  Duke,
who  played  a  great  part  in  the  events  of  the  time,  expressed  him-
self respecting  them.  One  may  here  look  for  important  and  decisive
explanations.

The  second  part  had  a  special  title  on  the  cover,  '  Life  of  H.R.H.
the  Duke  of  York  from  the  Restoration  of  Charles  II  to  his  death.'
The  inner  title  does  not  state  that  the  private  secretary  of  His  Royal
Highness  had  put  the  materials  together;  and  there  are  several
other  indications,  that  we  have  here  another  author  before  us.

First  of  all,  the  citations  from  the  original  memoirs  are  omitted ;  and
these  before  filled  the  margin  with  very  exact  references  to  the
passage  as  well  as  to  the  pages. In  the  section  between  1660  and

MEMOIRS  OF  JAMES  II.  33

1678  there  are  none  at  all;  not  until  after  that  do  they  begin
again.  A  new  form  of  citation  is  '  Letters,',  and  these  are  numbered
separately,  and  did  not  occur  in  the  earlier  portion.  While  in  the
first  part  the  Duke  was  introduced  for  the  most  part  as  speaking
in  the  first  person  (the  compiler  interposing  only  with  explanatory
remarks),  here  he  is  mentioned  in  the  third  person;  the  narrator
speaks  in  his  own  name.

If  we  turn  from  the  author  to  the  contents,  we  are  astonished
at  the  hostility  this  account  displays  towards,  the  administration  of
Lord  Clarendon,  and  at  its  divergence  from  the  section  in  Clarendon's
History,  in  which  this  topic  is  handled.  The  Lord  Chancellor,
although  not  without  some  personal  regret,  is  yet  censured  in  very
express  terms.

In  particular  it  is  charged  against  him  and  Southampton,  that
they  opposed  the  King's  intention  of  granting  the  Dissenters  a
modified  toleration,  whereby  the  King's  word  was  broken.  They
excited  people  against  the  King  without  arming  him;  they  even
neglected  to  make  his  person  secure  by  means  of  guards.  The
Chancellor  could  easily,  if  he  had  liked,  have  caused  the  repeal
of  all  the  laws  passed  by  the  Long  Parliament  to  the  detriment  of
the  crown ;  but  above  all,  he  could  and  ought  to  have  procured
for  the  King  a  better  revenue,  and  thus  have  made  him  independent
of  the  Parliament.  His  reason  probably  was — and  it  is  a  very  just
one — a  fear  of  the  King's  secret  predilection  for  Catholicism.

How  bitterly,  however,  did  the  wise  man  deceive  himself,  if  he
thought  that  by  the  institution  of  a  monarchy  dependent  on  himself,
and  by  the  marriage  of  his  daughter  with  the  heir  presumptive,
he  would  establish  his  power  for  ever;  it  was  precisely  this,  which
contributed  most  of  all  to  overthrow  it.

Strange  it  is  that  in  an  account,  based  on  the  notes  of  the  Duke
himself,  his  family  connexion  with  the  Chancellor  is  regarded  as
the  origin  of  his  misfortune.  Moreover,  this  is  specially  noted  as  the
cause  of  the  opposition  to  the  Duke  himself.  The  adversaries  of
the  Chancellor,  who  brought  about  his  overthrow,  feared  that  the
Duke  would  take  vengeance  on  them  for  this,  and  therefore  sought
to  free  themselves  from  him.

The  ministers  following,  Buckingham  and  Arlington,  Shaftesbury  as
well  as  Osborne  are  all  his  enemies,  they  fill  the  government  with
his  adversaries,  and  seek  to  exclude  him  from  the  succession,  having
conjectured  that  he  had  become  a  Catholic.

The  proceedings  of  the  Duke  in  the  two  Dutch  wars  are  described
with  considerable  minuteness,  for  above  all  things  it  is  to  be  made

RANKE,  VOL.  VI.  D

34  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL

patent,  that  he  devoted  himself  with  the  greatest  zeal  to  the  service
of  his  country.

The  author  then  relates  the  Duke's  secession  to  the  Catholic
Church,  which  is  narrated  with  more  exactness  and  detail  than  had
been  done  before.  This  step  of  the  Duke's  is  brought  into  con-
nexion with  the  project  of  introducing  Catholicism  into  England
generally,  a  connexion  which  has  found  admission  into  recent  accounts
of  these  events.  Hence  proceeded  the  decisions  of  Parliament,
the  Test  Act  of  1673,  even  the  attempt  of  the  Lords  in  1677  to
dissolve  the  Parliament,  the  plan  for  dissolving  the  King's  marriage,
but  above  all  the  putting  forward  of  Monmouth,  a  natural  son  of
Charles  II,  as  a  rival  to  the  Duke  ; — respecting  him  we  find  a  toler-
ably thorough  report.  Lastly  the  marriage  also  of  the  Prince  of  Orange
with  the  Duke's  daughter  is  noticed :  it  is  stated  that  it  was  proposed
without  his  foreknowledge  and  was  agreed  to  by  him,  in  order  to
show  that  he  had  no  intention  of  changing  the  government  and
religion  of  the  country.

It  is  patent,  how  very  personal  this  view  is.  The  national  religion
and  constitution  and  even  the  important  conjunctures  in  the  great
Commonwealth  of  Europe  are  scarcely  mentioned :  King  Charles
himself  appears  as  weak  and  hesitating :  among  the  statesmen
Clifford  alone  finds  favour ;  all  the  rest  are  depicted  as  enemies  and
half  traitors.

We  see  clearly,  that  we  have  here  no  history  of  this  period
before  us,  but  still  a  very  interesting  and  remarkable  contribution  to  it.

The  question  now  arises  for  the  historian,  how  far  he  can  make
use  of  this  information.  He  will  be  almost  scared  from  it,  when  he
notices  that  there  is  much  therein,  which  is  manifestly  false,  that
everywhere  a  very  interested  point  of  view  prevails,  and  that  precisely
here  citations  from  the  original  memoirs  fail  us.

We  have  here,  however,  an  independent  account,  which  is  of
immense  importance  in  forming  an  estimate  of  the  work  which  we
are  discussing.

As  already  mentioned,  long  before  it  appeared,  the  papers  existing
in  Paris,  which  since  then  (according  to  report)  have  been  lost,
excited  attention.  One  of  the  most  diligent  compilers  of  the  earlier
English  history  is  Thomas  Carte,  a  zealous  Jacobite,  who  was
compelled  to  leave  England  in  the  reign  of  George  I ;  later  on
he  ventured  to  return.  His  Life  of  the  Duke  of  Ormond,  which
appeared  in  three  folio  volumes  1735-37,  is  of  immense  importance
for  the  period  of  which  it  treats;  it  is  composed  entirely  from
the  Duke's  original  papers.  Carte  describes  how  he  found  the
most  considerable  portion  of  them,  and  had  them  taken  as  they  were

MEMOIRS  OF  JAMES  II  35

in  three  carts  to  Dublin,  for  in  Kilkenny  no  book-binder  was  to
be  found,  who  could  have  rendered  assistance  in  separating  and
arranging  them.  What  one  finds  in  Leland  respecting  this  time  is
compiled  from  Carte,  and  for  the  most  part  taken  word  for  word  from
him.  Carte's  view  was  directed  towards  a  description  of  the  time
succeeding  the  Restoration,  and  he  endeavoured  to  procure  authentic
material  for  it.  The  Fathers  in  the  Scottish  College  did  not  conceal
the  papers  from  so  decided  a  supporter  of  the  Stuarts,  Protestant
though  he  was:  he  made  extracts  from  them. and  brought  them  to
England.  He  died  in  1756,  before  he  had  made  use  of  them;  but
they  were  not  lost  in  consequence.  James  Macpherson  (he  to  whom
the  world  is  indebted  for  Ossian)  bought  them  of  Carte's  widow
and  then  went  himself  to  Paris,  in  order  to  complete  them.  He
made  use  of  them  in  an  historical  work;  but  this  time,  with  more
prudence  than  in  the  publication  of  the  Gaelic  poems,  he  had  his
authorities  printed  at  the  same  time.  No  one  has  ever  doubted
their  authenticity.

They  stand  now  at  the  very  beginning  under  the  decidedly  exag-
gerated title  of  '  Life  of  James  II  written  by  himself.'  The
extracts  are  signed  with  Carte's  name,  or  else,  where  additions  have
been  made  to  them,  with  Macpherson's  own.

Now  if  one  further  enquires  as  to  the  relation  in  which  these
stand  to  the  complete  biography  edited  by  Clarke,  one  arrives  at
the  result,  that  they  agree  in  the  order  of  the  narrative  and  the
matter  of  the  circumstances,  without  however  being  identical.

I  will  quote  a  few  instances.

In  the  account  of  the  conquest  of  New  Amsterdam,  which  hence-
forward was  called  New  York,  all  runs  the  same  even  down  to  certain
accidental  arrangements  of  words,  except  that  the  Life  says,  it
surrendered  'without  striking  a  stroke;'  in  the  extract  'without
being  blockaded.'  The  latter  is  the  more  correct.  Then  the
biography  goes  on  '  which  was  then  called  New  York,'  whereas  the
extracts  say  more  accurately,  referring  to  Nicholas,  the  English
commander  '  and  called  it  New  York ; '  so  that  the  name  is  expressly
attributed  to  Nicholas.

The  animosity  of  the  English  nation  on  account  of  the  unsuccessful
encroachments  of  the  Dutch  is  described  in  the  extracts  with  the
telling  words  '  All  that  people's  heads,  hearts,  and  purses  turned
that  way.'  The  biographer  says  more  quietly  '  it  now  grew  the
sense  of  that  whole  nation.'  He  says,  that  in  Holland  it  was  not
thought  necessary  to  give  satisfaction;  under  the  notion,  that  the
English  nation  would  not  plunge  so  deeply  into  a  naval  war,  especially
as it  was  only  a  short  time  since  peace  had  been  restored  at  home.

D  2

36  ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II

The  extract  is  here  beyond  all  doubt  more  correct ;  the  feeling  was
that  the  English  nation  would  not  mix  itself  up  in  the  quarrel  of
the  traders. For  it  was  primarily  a  strife  between  the  two  mercantile ,
companies,  and  the  question  undoubtedly  was,  whether  the  nation
would  then  take  part  in  it.

Divergences  of  this  kind  are  to  be  found  on  both  sides ;  the
extracts  are  not  taken  from  the  biography ;  but  the  latter  is  a  working
up  of  the  original  material  which  is  given  more  faithfully  in  the  extracts.

This  is  undoubtedly  the  true  state  of  the  case : — notes  by  James  II
lay  before  the  author  of  this  part  of  the  biography,  although  he  does
not  cite  them,  and  these  he  worked  in.  Carte  and  Macpherson  had
no  knowledge  of  the  existence  of  such  a  work :  they  made  use  of  the
autograph  notes  existing  in  the  Scottish  College ;  their  extracts  are
frequently  abbreviations ;  in  most  cases,  however,  they  are  true  copies
of  the  text  given  to  them.  That  they  are  so,  is  proved  by  their  not
unfrequent  verbal  agreement  with  the  work  of  the  biographer,  who
used  them  first,  and  who  was  rather  disposed  to  leave  out  than  to
add.  Where  however  he  ventures  to  do  the  tatter,  he  at  once
becomes  untrustworthy.

One  of  the  most  important  crises  in  the  history  of  the  time  is
the  marriage  of  the  Duke.  The  biography  is  here  much  more
detailed  than  the  extracts,  which  contain  only  a  few  notices.  I  can-
not, however,  believe,  that  more  existed  in  the  authentic  papers.
We  possess  an  authentic  report  on  the  subject  by  Lord  Peterborough,
who  concluded  the  betrothal  at  Modena.  In  the  very  rare  work  by
Halstead — Succinct  Genealogies  1685,  of  which  only  a  few  copies
are  in  existence  (one,  however,  in  the  British  Museum),  we  read  in
detail,  how  many  other  Princesses  were  considered,  whom  Lord  Peter-
borough was  commissioned  to  visit,  in  order  to  give  a  favourable
or  unfavourable  report  respecting  them.  The  Princess  of  Modena
pleased  him  more  than  any.  One  sees  further,  that  the  betrothal
of  the  heir  presumptive  to  the  throne  of  England  to  a  Princess  of
the  house  of  Este  was  very  unwelcome  to  the  Roman  court,  because
it  gave  that  house  a  support,  which  was  not  looked  upon  with  satis-
faction at  Rome :  Lord  Peterborough  concluded  the  engagement  on
his  own  authority  beforehand,  and  the  Pope  merely  gave  an  after-
approval.  All  this  is  undoubted.  The  biographer  is  not  only  not
aware  of  it,  but  he  even  ascribes  the  consent  of  the  young  Princess
to  the  exhortations  of  the  Pope.  These,  he  says,  were  conveyed
to  her  by  her  mother ;  '  with  much  difficulty  His  Holiness  and  Her
Highness  prevailed  upon  the  princess.'  Later  on  people  might
regard  the  result  of  the  affair  in  this  light ;  in  reality  the  facts  were
not  such ;  the  extracts  also  contain  nothing  of  the  kind.

ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II 37

Of  still  greater  importance  is  the  question,  whether  the  account,
which  the  biographer  gives  of  the  origin  of  the  Catholic  project  in
the  year  1669  and  1670,  agrees  with  the  extracts,  and  can  in  general
be  accepted.

The  chief  fact  is  a  conversation,  which  took  place  between  the
Duke  and  the  Jesuit  Father  Joseph  Symond  (Simons)  in  the
beginning  of  1669.  This  is  all  perfectly  right.  The  original  nar-
rative is  extant;  the  biographer  has  merely  employed  the  third
person  instead  of  the  first.  Here,  however,  a  correction  suggests
itself.  The  biographer  begins  by  saying,  that  the  Duke  had  been
long  of  opinion,  that  the  Church  of  England  was  the  true
Church,  which  is  sense  only  in  so  far  as  it  might  imply  his  after-
wards acknowledging  that  such  an  opinion  was  wrong.  Hence  one
would  necessarily  expect  a  refutation  of  such  a  belief,  but  of  this  there
is  no  trace.  On  the  contrary  the  Duke  says  in  the  original,  that  he
has  long  been  of  opinion  that  the  Roman  Church  is  the  true  one.
'  Having  long  had  in  my  thought  that  the  Church  of  Rome  was
the  only  true  one;'  whereupon  he  proceeds  at  once  to  declare
that  he  wishes  to  become  a  Catholic  and  to  be  reconciled  to  the
Church.  Father  Symond  tells  him,  that  in  that  case  he  must
separate  from  the  Protestant  Church,  for  not  even  the  Pope  could
give  him  leave  to  be  externally  a  Protestant  and  internally  a  Catholic.

This  is  the  thought  which  determines  the  whole  bearing  of  James  ;
for  several  years  he  still  did  not  become  a  Catholic.  In  a  report  of
the  Abbe  Falconieri  in  the  year  1674  it  is  said,  that  from  the  behaviour
of  the  Prince  people  had  seen,  that  he  must  have  become  a  Catholic  ;
he  had  enquired,  when  this  took  place,  and  had  learned,  that  the  change
took  place  in  the  year  1672,  before  the  Duke  took  command  of  the  fleet.
Of  this  neither  the  Life  nor  the  extracts  have  any  distinct  notice.  It
was  accomplished  probably  by  a  chaplain  of  the  Queen-mother.  At
any  rate  one  of  these  told  the  Abbe*  Falconieri  so,  and  he  then  re-
peated the  statement  in  his  report  to  A.  Altieri  in  Rome.  I  found
the  letter  some  time  ago  in  the  Altieri  Palace.

Let  us  now  return  to  the  year  1669.

The  biographer  says,  that  the  Duke  thereupon  spoke  to  the  King,
and  the  latter  also  declared  that  he  had  determined  to  become  a
Catholic;  a  formal  deliberation  was  held  on  Jan.  25th,  the  Con-
version of  S.  Paul,  as  to  the  best  means  of  restoring  Catholicism ;  the
King  then  expressed  himself  decisively,  and  it  was  determined  to
apply  to  France;  the  French  ambassador  Colbert  Croissy  was  first
taken  into  the  secret,  and  then  Lord  Arundel  was  sent  to  France.

If  this  had  been  the  case,  Croissy,  all  of  whose  reports  I  have  seen,
would  have  said  something  about  it. But  on  the  contrary Colbert

38  ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II.

Croissy  was  purposely  kept  in  the  dark  about  these  plans,  which  were
not  made  known  to  him  until  three  months  later,  and  then  by
Louis  XIV ;  for  Charles  II  was  still  against  it.

The  matter  is  mentioned  in  the  extracts,  but  in  a  milder,  less
decided  way;  according  to  this  the  Duke  in  1668,  on  resuming
friendly  relations  with  the  King  after  some  estrangement,  turned  the
conversation  on  religion,  and  the  King  replied,  that  he  wished  for
nothing  more  than  'to  be  reconciled'  to  the  Church.  Probably  this
was  what  induced  the  Duke  to  cause  a  Jesuit  priest  to  be  called.  On
his  declaration  it  was  decided,  that  a  complete  break  with  the  Pro-
testant Church  was  necessary,  and  accordingly  the  consultation  above-
mentioned  was  held.  The  extracts  agree  in  placing  it  on  the  25th  of
January,  the  day  chosen  on  account  of  its  good  auspices  by  the
spiritual  advisers,  with  whom  the  Duke  had  become  acquainted  during
his  wife's  illness.  The  object  was  to  come  to  an  understanding  re-
specting the  means  of  introducing  Catholicism  into  the  kingdom ;
the  King  spoke  for  it  with  enthusiasm,  for  he  had  always  had  an
inclination  that  way ;  and  it  was  decided  that  France  should  be
consulted  respecting  the  preliminary  steps.

It  will  of  course  be  ascribed  merely  to  the  zeal  of  the  biographer,
that  he  makes  Charles  II  with  tears  in  his  eyes  declare  himself  a
Catholic.  He  makes  him  say,  they  must  behave  as  becomes  good
Catholics.

But  it  had  not  yet  come  to  that;  far  from  it.  The  secession  of
the  King  never  followed,  at  least  not  before  the  moment  of  death  ;
and  that  of  the  Duke  not  until  several  years  later  than  the  time  in
question.  There  was  no  mention  of  a  bona  fide  secession,  merely
of  a  tendency  that  way,  which  in  the  case  of  the  King  takes  the
form  of  fitful  paroxysms  of  devotion  and  penitence.

The  result  of  the  small  consultation  on  Jan.  25  was  by  no  means
a  resolution  to  break  with  Protestantism,  but  only  to  make  such
preparations  by  means  of  an  alliance  with  France,  on  which  Charles
II  fell  back  in  any  case,  as  to  render  the  thing  possible  in  the
future.

After  all  that  we  have  remarked  no  one  could  suppose,  that  the
biography  can  possibly  be  the  work  of  James  II.  It  is  not  how-
ever wholly  untrue  to  say  that  to  a  certain  extent  it  originates
from  him.  It  is  based  on  autobiographical  notes  and  other  authen-
tic material.  This  fact  having  been  placed  beyond  a  doubt  by
Carte's  and  Macpherson's  extracts,  we  are  able  by  the  same  means
to  test  the  work  of  the  biographer.  Where  he  proceeds  alone,  he
deserves  no  consideration ;  one  must  everywhere  refer  to  the  ex-
tracts. These,  however,  acquire  all  the  greater  value. If  the  common

ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II  39

story  is  true,  and  the  originals  have  really  perished,  then  Carte's
and  Macpherson's  extracts  are  all  that  remains  of  James  IFs  own
memoirs ;  at  any  rate  they  are  so  for  us.

They  are  not  at  all  systematically  arranged;  only  here  and
there  does  one  see  in  Carte's  extracts  an  approach  to  a  journal.
For  the  most  part  they  are  memoranda  casually  put  on  to  paper,
just  as  they  came,  or  were  introduced  in  conversation.  One
stumbles  on  repetitions  and  corrections.  Macpherson's  supple-
mentary extracts  are  on  the  whole  very  sparse  in  this  period,  and,
where  they  do  appear,  approximate  to  the  biography ;  still  there  are
many  facts,  which  are  introduced  into  the  biography,  but  are  not
found  in  it.  I  shall  not  attempt  to  decide  whether  they  are  the
result  of  a  compilation,  or  belong  to  the  original  notes.

On  the  whole  the  extracts  also  have  been  made  by  no  means  so  care-
fully, and  are  by  no  means  so  trustworthy  as  one  could  have  wished.

Let  us  now  cast  a  look  upon  the  portions  of  the  work  which
follow.

From  a  passage  in  the  second  volume,  where  the  likeness  of  the
Pretender  ('His  present  Majesty')  to  the  King,  his  father,  and  the
Queen,  his  mother,  is  quoted  as  proof  of  his  legitimacy,  it  has  been
argued,  that  the  whole  biographical  wrork  was  not  composed  until
perhaps  the  first  decad  of  the  18th  century.  That  cannot  be  true
of  the  section  thus  far  considered,  which  has  no  citations  ;  in  the
title  page  James  II  is  spoken  of  by  his  title  of  Duke.  From  the
next  section,  however,  to  which  I  am  now  coming,  one  might
easily  suppose  this.  James  III,  if  one  may  call  him  so,  asked
the  Scottish  College  for  his  father's  papers  from  the  year  1678.
It  is  precisely  at  this  year  that  a  new  composition  begins,  dis-
tinguished by  its  form  from  the  rest,  in  that  abundant  citations
appear  once  more,  not  merely  from  the  memoirs,  but  also  from
the  correspondence  between  Charles  II  and  James  II;  from  the
latter  many  passages  are  quoted  verbatim;  from  the  former  a
number  of  narratives  have  been  taken.  In  the  first  division,  ac-
cording to  our  arrangement,  the  biographer  made  use  of  fully
elaborated  memoirs ;  in  the  second  he  made  use  of  memoranda,
which  he  proceeded  to  put  into  shape  himself;  while  in  the  third
one  sees  a  collector,  who  has  various  materials  in  manuscript  before
him,  and  even  quotes  from  what  is  in  print.  This  part  begins
with  the  papist  conspiracy,  the  Titus-Oates-plot  of  1678.  The
point  of  view  taken  is,  that  the  denuntiations  at  that  time  were  not
merely  nugatory  and  fictitious,  but  also  were  in  fact  directed  against
the  Duke.  The  narrative  here  as  before  abstains  from  giving  a
general  view; it confines itself  to an exclusively  personal stand-

40  ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II.

point; enmity  to the Duke  determines the measure  of  the pro-
ceedings which  are  assigned  to  each  individual.

The  materials  denoted  by  references  and  marks  of  quotation  at
the  side  form  a  very  considerable  portion  of  this  section.  The
inserted  narratives  of  James  II  are  very  detailed;  they  are  en-
larged by  the  contents  of  the  letters ;  there  are  isolated  notes  of
his  from  the  time  of  his  own  reign,  which  here  and  there  are  of  value.

Now  if  we  ask  to  begin  with,  in  what  relation  the  extracts  stand
to  this  work,  the  answer  is  that  they  are  found  to  be  independent  of  it
and  useful  even  when  placed  side  by  side  with  such  a  detailed  biography.
Sometimes  they  agree  verbally  with  the  received  text,  not  unfrequently
(and  this  is  remarkable)  just  where  references  and  notes  of  quotation
are  wanting; — yet  even  here  there  are  small  touches,  which  the  bio-
grapher has  overlooked,  e.  g.  when  the  readmission  of  the  Duke  of
Buckingham  to  the  King's  favour  (the  effect  of  which  upon  Danby  is
rated  very  highly  in  the  biography)  is  attributed  in  the  extracts  to  the
influence  of  Nell  Gwyn,  the  King's  Protestant  mistress :  sometimes
the  extracts  are  more  detailed  and  essentially  better/ than  the  accounts
given  in  the  biography,  e.  g.  in  the  case  of  the  hasty  return  of  the
Duke  from  Brussels  to  Windsor  in  September  1679.

With  regard  to  this  journey  the  extracts  are  fairly  exact  in  their
agreement  with  the  biography,  but  on  a  more  important  topic — the
attitude  of  the  court  on  this  occasion — they  differ  from  it.  The  ex-
tract are  in  this  connexion  more  detailed  and  exact.  According
to  the  extracts  a  letter  of  Sunderland's  first  arrived  with  news  of  the
illness,  and  yet  at  the  same  time  with  an  exhortation  to  the  Duke  to
come  :  a  similar  one  from  Feversham ;  but  immediately  afterwards
an  express  brings  the  Duke  an  order  to  present  himself.  The
leading  men,  Sunderland,  Halifax,  Godolphin,  called  the  Duchess  of
Portsmouth  to  counsel  along  with  the  friends  of  the  Duke,  Hyde,  and
Feversham ;  it  was  agreed,  that  the  Duke  was  to  be  summoned ;
thereupon  the  King  was  asked  about  it,  and  '  the  king  on
proposal  agreed  to  it.'  In  the  biography  all  proceeds  from  the
King :  '  the  king  finding  himself  worse,  ordered  the  Duke  of  Sun-
derland, &c.'  But  the  position  of  affairs  is  dislocated  thereby.  For
it  was  a  coalition  of  the  persons  dominant  at  court,  to  the  exclusion
of  Monmouth,  by  whom  the  Duke  was  summoned.

The  account  of  the  return  of  Monmouth  in  November  1679  is
given  in  the  extracts  from  original  notes  in  a  much  more  detailed
and  interesting  way  than  in  the  biography.

There  are  two  accounts  in  the  extracts  of  the  fresh  removal  of
the  Duke  from  court  in  the  year  1680,  of  which  one  plainly  sets
forth  the  objects  of  the  various  more  influential  persons,  such  as

ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II  41

Sunderland  and  the  Duchess  of  Portsmouth,  and  in  particular  notices
a  coalition  of  that  lady  with  Shaftesbury,  (p.  104);  this  account
is  passed  over  in  the  biography  and  another  set  forth,  in  which
these  facts  are  wanting,  but  which  nevertheless  contains  various
other  details.

In  the  account  of  the  proceedings  which  preceded  the  second  return
of  the  Duke  to  court,  it  appears  in  the  biography,  as  if  the  mission
of  Laurence  Hyde  to  Edinburgh  in  August  1681,  which  is  said  to
have  made  the  Duke's  conformity  a  condition  of  his  return,  had
for  its  object  to  keep  him  at  a  distance;  the  zealous  Catholic
writer  loads  the  Duke  with  praises,  because  he  prefers  to  endure
this,  rather  than  make  the  smallest  concession.

He  had  a  note  before  him  here,  which  is  preserved  in  the  extracts,
and  manifestly  comes  from  a  written  or  verbal  narrative  of  James  II.
The  King  let  the  Duke  know,  that  unless  he  conformed  he  would
not  be  able  to  support  him  any  longer,  as  he  had  hitherto  done ;  the
Duke  would  'ruin  himself  and  him'  (the  King).  It  is  a  proof  of  the
biographer's  re-touching,  that  he  expresses  it  in  this  way; — that  the
King  had  struggled  hard  to  defend  him,  but  now,  unless  he  yielded,
not  only  he  but  the  King  also  would  be  ruined.  This  form  destroys
the  original  mode  of  expression.  In  the  original  it  goes  on  to  say
that  Hyde  had  done  all  to  accomplish  his  object,  and  had  represented
'the  originall  state  of  affaires;'  the  biographer  repeats  the  first  words,
but  makes  him  then  speak  of  '  the  dismal  situation  of  His  Royall
Highness,  if  he  did  not  acquiess  to  the  King's  request  and  reso-
lution;' but  this  certainly  was  not  the  author's  meaning.  The  bio-
grapher lauds  his  hero,  because  he  withstood  this  temptation  to  his
everlasting  fame; — that  was  just  his  character;  never  had  Christian
steadfastness  and  determination  endured  a  severer  conflict;  it  was
a  work  for  the  welfare  of  the  oecumenical  Church.  The  main  fact,
however,  is  rather  obscured ;  it  lies  in  this,  that  Charles  II  first  sent
to  require  the  Duke  to  conform  entirely,  and  then  merely  insisted
that  he  should  consent  to  attend  public  worship.  The  omission  of
these  words  makes  the  whole  unintelligible.

After  this  proof  it  might  seem  as  if  one  could  set  aside  the  work  of
the  biographer  altogether  :  that,  however,  is  not  the  case.  He  gives
at  the  same  time  a  citation  from  a  letter  from  Lord  Halifax,  which  is  of
the  greatest  importance  with  regard  to  this  remarkable  statesman  and
to  the  whole  situation.  One  sees  from  it,  that  Halifax,  although  a
great  champion  for  the  succession  of  the  Duke,  did  not  on  that
account  allow  himself  to  be  moved  to  make  concessions  to  Catho-
licism, for  negotiations  of  that  kind  were  not  begun  with  his  approval  ;
and  this  throws  a  certain  amount  of  light  on  the  later  bearing  of  this
exceedingly  influential  statesman.

42  ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II

In  general  the  extracts  acquire  a  special  value  as  they  quote
letters,  which  the  Duke  received,  while  absent  from  London,  from
Hyde,  Seymour,  Conway,  and  others,  whose  names  do  not  appear.
One  recognises  these  passages,  which  are  frequently  not  distinguished
from  the  rest  of  the  text,  by  the  words  '  to-morrow/  '  yesterday ; '  or
by  the  remark,  that  this  or  that  is  expected  next.  In  the  biography
they  are  made  use  of  for  the  most  part,  but  not  always.

When  one  puts  together  these  extracts,  and  the  notes  and  statements
out  of  letters  which  are  interwoven  with  the  biography,  the  amount
due  to  the  personal  authorship  of  James  II  is  considerable,  and
deserves  the  attention  of  the  historian.

It  is  essential  that  the  two  should  be  put  together.

Some  years  ago  I  was  reproached  with  writing  history  out  of  scraps.
Certainly  I  do  not,  so  long  as  detailed  informants  hold  out.  But  when
the  originals  are  either  lost,  or  are  kept  concealed,  it  is  absolutely
necessary  to  make  use  of  less  perfect  accounts  and  fragmentary
communications.  It  is  just  at  such  points  that  cases  are  wont  to
occur,  which  are  purposely  kept  dark,  and  which  are  among  the
most  important.

This  is  possible  with  regard  to  the  fragments  incorporated  with  the
biography,  because  it  is  evident  that  they  are  given,  not  indeed  verbally,
but  in  sense.  One  has  only  to  be  on  one's  guard  against  the  colour,
which  is  imparted  to  them.  In  the  biography  composition  and
description  are  in  the  highest  degree  one-sided  and  partial.

It  is  based  on  the  idea,  which  the  Jesuit  Father  Orleans  has
expressed  in  his  '  Revolutions  in  England,'  a  book  which  had  already
appeared  in  the  lifetime  of  James.  He  saw  in  him  a  perfect  Catholic
and  Christian  prince,  and  declares  that  he  defended  his  rights  to  the
Crown  with  a  courage  which*  astonished  his  enemies,  but  prized
religion  so  highly,  that  he  on  the  other  hand  held  these  rights  cheap
and  risked  them  for  it  (iii.  p.  360).  And  this  is  pretty  much  the
light  in  which  the  matter  is  regarded  in  the  biography.

The  description  which  is  given  of  the  reign  of  James  II  is  of  less
value.

The  memoirs  are  seldom  mentioned,  letters  (so  far  as  I  can  discover)
not  at  all.  On  the  other  hand  scattered  notes  of  James  appear —
1  King  James'  loose  sheets/  '  loose  papers/ — which  contain  some  original
matter.  Still  this  vanishes  under  the  influence  of  the  object  of  the
narrative,  which  is  directed  towards  making  the  blame  of  all  that  mis-
carried fall  on  the  first  Minister,  Sunderland.

According  to  this  account,  Sunderland  was  in  danger  at  first ;  in
order  to  maintain  himself,  he  unites  with  Rochester,  with  the  full
expectation  that  his  Anglican  bearing  would  alienate  Rochester  from

ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II.  43

the  King ;  so  when  that  takes  place,  he  causes  the  King  to  form  a
.  Catholic  council,  to  which  all  business  is  transferred,  but  which  is
again  ruled  by  Sunderland.  Even  the  coming  forward  of  Father
Petre  is  traced  to  this  policy ;  Sunderland  had,  it  is  said,  praised  him
to  the  King,  and  the  latter  was  glad  to  see  that  a  man  like  Father
Petre  was  valued  by  a  statesman  like  Sunderland.

It  is  an  interesting  question,  whether  later  on  this  was  not  the
King's  own  idea.

I  think  that  one  may  believe  this;  for  one  finds  it  in  the  extracts
also,  which  here,  if  one  follows  the  wording,  have  the  greatest
originality,  and  are  probably  taken  likewise  from  the  loose  sheets,
which  the  biographer  mentions.  When,  for  instance,  it  is  said  of
Father  Petre,  '  Petre  was  a  plausible,  but  a  weak  man,  abounding  in
words ; '  that  is  without  doubt  the  basis  of  the  words  in  the  biography,
1  he  was  indeed  a  plausible,  but  a  weak  man ;  he  hath  only  the  art  by
abundance  of  words  to  port  a  gloss  upon  a  weak  and  shallow  judg-
ment.' But  where  the  biography  and  extracts  agree,  one  can  be
pretty  sure  that  King  James  is  the  original  author.  In  the  last  book
of  Father  Orleans,  who  got  information  from  the  King,  one  can  read
this  almost  word  for  word  (148).  In  the  extracts  it  is  said  :  'he  was
made  a  privy  counsellor,  contrary  to  his  own  (the  King's)  judgment,
and  the  Queen's  advice.'  That  has  been  copied  word  for  word  into
the  biography,  merely  with  the  addition,  that  the  Queen  had  based  her
advice  simultaneously  on  the  rules  of  the  Jesuits.  Father  Orleans  says
the  King  did  it :  '  malgre  lui  meme,  malgre'  le  conseil  qui  s'y  opposoit,
malgre  les  plus  effectives  loix  de  l'ordre  dont  6toit  ce  pere'  (423).

Now  although  King  James  most  probably  afterwards  shared  these
views,  yet  he  would  scarcely  have  approved  of  a  dissertation,  such  as
follows  in  the  biography  j  he  himself  appears  altogether  pitiable  therein
and  still  less  self-reliant  than  he  was.  After  a  mishap  has  occurred,  it
is  a  very  common  excuse,  that  a  prince  allowed  this  or  that  to  happen
through  mistrusting  his  own  judgment ;  here  it  is  peculiarly  mis-
applied, for  the  direction  followed  was  entirely  the  King's  own.

Sunderland  is  regarded  as  having  an  understanding  with  the  Prince
of  Orange,  from  whom  he  had  drawn  money  ;  the  Prince  of  Orange  is
depicted  as  an  old  secret  enemy.  No  doubt  is  entertained  that  he
took  part  in  the  first  attempt  of  Monmouth  and  Argyle;  what  was
conjectured  at  the  time,  is  recognised  as  confirmed  by  the  result.

Most  of  the  transactions  of  the  King  which  history  condemns  are
noted  in  this  biographical  work  also  as  errors.  One  could  almost  wish
that  an  attempt  had  been  made  to  justify  them,  because  one  would
then  learn  something  of  the  actual  motives  which  were  at  work  in
each  crisis;  one  feels  the  want  of  notes  made  at  the  moment.

44  ON  THE  AUTOBIOGRAPHY  OF  JAMES  II.

The  dissertation  on  the  right  of  dispensation  (ii.  82),  is  an  extract
from  an  apologetic  paper  by  the  Chief  Justice,  who  was  attacked
because  he  supported  it.  Hume  also  has  drawn  from  this  paper,  and
certainly  in  a  far  better  way  than  our  biographer.

In  the  narration  of  events  deviations  from  the  truth  occur  here  and
there,  which  may  be  the  result  of  ignorance ;  but  the  circumstances,
which  one  assumes,  ought  at  the  same  time  to  serve  as  an  excuse.
Thus  in  a  speech,  which  Father  Orleans  and  the  biographer  report  in
the  same  way,  the  assurance  is  contained,  that  Parliament  was  already
summoned  again,  at  a  time  when  (according  to  authentic  documents)
this  was  certainly  not  the  case.

Where  we  are  sufficiently  informed  respecting  personal  circum-
stances, e.g.  the  audience  of  the  Bishops,  Nov.  6,  1688,  as  to  which
an  account  by  the  Bishop  of  Rochester  is  extant,  the  narrations  of  the
biographer,  for  which  the  authority  of  James  II  is  quoted,  agree  in
general  with  the  Bishop,  yet  seem  more  like  recollections  long  after
the  event ;  they  lack  the  colour  of  direct  testimony  and  of  complete
trustworthiness.

The  fourth  part  (on  the  title-page  of  which  it  is  not  stated  that  it  is
drawn  from  the  memoirs  of  James  II)  presents  a  series  of  articles,
which  profess  to  be  taken  from  the  memoirs ;  according  to  the  notes
in  the  margin  they  come  from  the  ninth  volume  of  '  King  James'
Memoires.'  They  are  to  a  great  extent  on  English  affairs,  and  in
particular  on  the  connexions,  which  this  prince  kept  up  there ;  chiefly,
however,  on  the  war  in  Ireland.  James  II  caused  several  reports  of  it
to  be  elaborated,  and  sent  them  to  the  French  court ;  those  extant  in
the  biography  have  a  certain  family  likeness  to  these,  but  do  not
entirely  agree  with  them.  In  %Macpherson's  extracts  there  are  some
passages  which  agree  word  for  word.  He  somewhere  remarks,  that
they  come  from  a  life  of  James  II,  not  written  by  him,  but  which  he
had  perused.  And  this  may  well  be  the  case  with  many  others  also.
Here,  where  the  general  view  taken  does  not  come  into  question,  this
being  determined  rather  by  the  situation  of  an  exiled  prince,  the
biography  has  great  value. Here  and  there  its  statements  are  decisive.

If  I  might  venture  to  put  together  the  results  of  this  investigation,
the  following  is  what  we  arrive  at : —

(1)  The  idea  of  a  continuous  memoir  by  James  II  cannot  be
entertained.

(2)  The  most  detailed  accounts  written  either  by  himself  or  under
his  guidance  are  of  a  military  character,  and  have  reference  to  the
campaigns  in  which  he  served  under  Turenne,  and  to  the  war  in
Ireland  after  his  flight.

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 45

(3)  All  the  rest,  especially  all  that  has  reference  to  the  period  from
1660  to  1688,  the  most  important  of  any,  is  written  very  frag-
mentarily  and  without  method,  just  as  opportunities  and  chances
occurred,  and  that  not  in  any  case  by  himself,  but  by  one  of  his
secretaries.

(4)  These  are  the  materials  from  which  the  Life  of  James  is  com-
piled, which,  as  being  derived  from  papers  left  by  the  house  of  Stuart,
and  edited  after  transmission  to  England  by  Clarke,  is  frequently
mentioned  as  a  memoir  by  James  himself.  The  various  portions  of
it  are  the  work  of  various  periods,  written  in  various  styles  and
manners ;  the  earlier  portions  before  his  accession,  the  later,  from
1678  onwards,  not  written  till  after  the  death  of  King  James,  at  the
wish  and  command  of  his  son.

(5)  The  materials  themselves,  however,  are  to  some  extent  not  lost,
inasmuch  as  the  custodians  of  them  twice  allowed  extracts  to  be  made
from  them.  These  extracts  are  in  some  cases  actual  abbreviations;
in  most  cases,  however,  they  are  copies  of  isolated  passages,  these
themselves  forming  no  complete  whole.

(6)  They  are  of  much  importance,  if  for  nothing  else,  because  in
them  the  original  form  is  better  preserved  than  in  the  detailed  bio-
graphy; besides  which,  they  contain  much  that  has  been  passed
over  in  the  biography.

(7)  In  the  biography  also  there  is  much  that  is  wanting  in  the
extracts ;  not  until  one  has  put  the  two  together  does  the  extent  of
the  original  notes  and  materials  appear.  They  are  specially  of  value
for  the  period  between  1678  and  1685,  a  time  of  the  greatest  party-
agitation,  respecting  which  we  here  find  extracts  and  confidential
correspondence  not  known  elsewhere.

The  biography  is  very  far  from  containing  a  history  of  this  time.
It  is  one-sided,  partial,  personal;  still  it  gives  valuable  information,
which  forms  a  real  contribution  to  the  history  of  this  epoch.  One  is
indebted  to  the  memory  of  George  IV  for  the  publication  of  them.

III.

BURNET'S HISTORY  OF HIS OWN TIMES.

With  clerical  pathos  Burnet  assures  us  that  his  intention  is  not  to
gratify  the  world  with  the  disclosure  of  secrets  and  write  an  entertain-
ing book,  but  something  better  and  deeper ;  he  wished  to  show  the
errors  of  governments,  the  follies  of  parties,  in  order  to  make  the  next
generation  better.  He  calls  the  God  of  truth  to  witness  that  he  will
speak  the  truth,  so  far  as  he  has  been  able  to  discover  it.

4  6 BURNET 'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

The  world  has  not  allowed  his  claim ;  his  History  is  regarded
merely  as  an  entertaining  one ;  it  is  precisely  with  regard  to  its
truthfulness  that  the  most  vigorous  opposition  has  been  raised
against  it.

And  how  can  any  one,  who  proposes  to  write  the  history  of  his  own
time,  escape  this  charge  ?  It  is  the  most  far-reaching,  the  most  am-
bitious, but  for  one's  own  reputation  the  most  perilous  undertaking  on
which  an  author  who  is  concerned  about  truth  can  venture.  Here
what  is  far  off  must  be  introduced,  no  less  than  what  is  near,  in  the
manner  of  Thuanus,  to  whose  example  Burnet  sometimes  refers ;  of  a
comprehension  of  the  state  of  affairs  in  the  world  at  large,  such  as
Thuanus  attempted,  there  is,  however,  in  Burnet  scarcely  the  faintest
trace.  He  keeps  to  the  province  of  Scottish  and  English  affairs,  with
which  he  unites  those  of  Holland  and  France,  but  only  so  far  as  these
affect  the  former,  and  as  they  came  to  his  knowledge  by  staying  in
those  countries.  He  undertook  to  write  the  history  of  Great  Britain
during  fifty  years,  from  1660  to  17 10  ;  but  he  has  exceeded  these  limits
at  both  ends.  The  chief  subject  of  his  description  is  the  Revolution
of  1688,  how  it  was  brought  about,  and  what  resulted  from  it  under
King  William  and  Queen  Anne.  These  are  affairs  which  affect  him
immediately,  in  which  he  himself  played  a  part.  But  how  much  self-
denial  is  needed,  to  narrate  with  objective  impartiality  events,  in  which
one  has  oneself  taken  part,  to  do  justice  to  one's  opponents,  to  appre-
ciate their  motives ;  and  how  difficult  it  is  at  the  same  time,  seeing  that
no  one  stands  always  at  the  centre  of  occurrences,  to  find  that  out
also,  in  which  one  had  taken  no  part,  and  which  perhaps  has  been
purposely  kept  concealed.  In  historical  works  of  this  kind  the  personal
element  will  prevail ;  a  man  will  not  desert  in  his  writings  the  party  to
which  he  belongs  in  his  life.  But  even  so  such  works  are  in  the
highest  degree  welcome  to  those  who  come  after,  so  far  as  they  faith-
fully record  the  experiences  of  the  author.  They  cannot  contain  the
whole  of  history,  but  still  some  portion  of  it,  according  to  the  degree
in  which  the  author  was  called  to  share  and  participate  in  it.

The  first  question  then  always  is,  what  position  he  held  in  it.  The
limits,  which  confine  all  personal  relations,  give  the  true  means  of
criticising  any  historical  performance  which  has  a  general  character.

Let  me  be  allowed  one  more  preliminary  remark.

However  closely  what  is  private  and  what  is  historical  in  persons
may  be  connected,  one  can  still,  it  seems  to  me,  separate  them.  The
former  depends  upon  the  general  conditions  of  life,  the  family,  the
special  pursuit  and  business,  the  office  which  a  man  holds,  his  natural
temperament :  the  latter  is  something  quite  different ;  it  depends  upon
the  attitude  which  a  man  assumes  towards  the  great  questions  that

BURNET S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 47

occupy  and  agitate  the  century  to  which  he  belongs,  and  upon  the
degree  in  which  he  is  able  to  realise  his  conceived  idea ;  it  is  his  posi-
tion in  the  intellectual  sphere.  The  more  profoundly  general  relations
are  grasped,  the  more  they  are  developed  in  the  conflicts  of  the  time
and  in  view  of  questions  under  solution,  so  much  the  more  do  they
penetrate  the  individual  life :  a  fact  which  imparts  to  life  a  new  and
peculiar  value.  The  degree,  in  which  a  man  finds  room  for  the  prin-
ciples which  he  professes,  in  his  writings  or  his  life,  constitutes  the
historical  personality  which  abides  in  remembrance.

Burnet  was  born  at  Edinburgh  in  1643,  and  developed  very  rapidly
under  his  father's  instruction,  so  that  he  became  Master  of  Arts  in  his
fourteenth  year,  and  took  his  intellectual  line  in  life  in  the  first  years  of
the  Restoration  in  England,  like  many  other  notable  men  of  the  time.

The  storms  of  the  Civil  War,  of  the  Protectorate,  and  of  the  attempts
at  a  republican  form  of  government,  which  preceded  these  years,  were
over.  Gilbert  Burnet,  like  Locke,  belonged  to  those  who  greeted  the
restoration  of  the  monarchy  with  joy.  His  mother  was  sister  of  one
of  the  most  important  and  most  effective  leaders  of  the  Covenanting  ■
party,  Archibald  Johnstoun,  who  was  raised  to  be  Lord  Warriston;
only  Johnstoun  was  not  master  of  his  nearest  relatives.  The  father  of
Burnet,  his  brother-in-law,  had  refused  to  subscribe  the  League  and
Covenant,  and  went  into  exile  rather  than  be  associated  with  it.  And
it  was  not  to  the  uncle,  who  had  to  pay  for  the  success  and  brilliancy
of  his  undertakings  with  his  life,  and  leave  a  numerous  family — he
had  thirteen  children — in  great  poverty,  but  to  the  principles  of  his
father  that  Gilbert  Burnet  attached  himself;  like  him,  without  being
one  of  the  followers  of  Charles  I,  he  held  fast  to  the  opinion,  that  the
rising  of  the  Scots  was  not  justified.  Although  Burnet  in  the  be-
ginning of  his  narrative  of  events  under  the  Restoration  does  justice
to  the  Presbyterians  in  other  respects,  yet  he  finds  fault  with  their  doc-
trine of  the  Church's  independence  of  the  civil  power,  their  proneness
to  condemn  the  sins  of  Princes  and  Lords,  which  pleases  men  as  an
act  of  candour,  while  it  does  not  touch  themselves,  and  their  zeal
always  ready  to  incite  the  populace  to  tumult  and  disobedience  (I.  261).
The  Papacy  had  from  of  old  been  blamed  for  its  contests  with  the
royal  power.  Burnet  maintains  that  the  opposition  of  the  zealous
Presbyterians  to  the  Crown  is  still  more  dangerous.  He  rejected  the
Covenant  as  irreconcileable  with  the  Monarchy.

But  the  characteristic  of  the  Restoration  lay  in  this,  that  not  merely
the  Monarchy  but  also  the  Episcopal  system  was  re-established ;  this
was  the  most  important  result  of  Clarendon's  conduct  of  affairs.  And
Lord  Middleton,  who  conducted  the  administration  of  Scotland  during
the  first  years,  was  as  zealous  for  it  as  Lord  Clarendon  ever  was.

48 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

Under  the  fresh  impulse  of  royalist  feeling  the  Scottish  Parliament
was  won  over  to  vote  for  it ;  that  system,  against  which  the  first  rising
of  the  Scots  had  been  directed,  was  re-established.  The  Bishops,
consecrated  in  England  according  to  the  rule  of  the  Church,  returned
in  all  pomp  back  to  their  sees.

With  this  Burnet  was  not  so  well  pleased.  He  had  studied  the
Fathers  of  the  first  centuries,  for  he  had  a  natural  instinct,  confirmed
by  study,  always  to  go  back  to  first  sources.  In  them  he  found  of
course  the  Episcopate,  yet  not  one  adorned  with  worldly  dignity  and
riches,  but  an  office  of  preaching  and  the  cure  of  souls.  A  stay  in
Cambridge  had  a  great  influence  on  Burnet,  owing  to  the  teaching  of
the  theologico-philosophical  School,  wHich  arose  there  at  that  time.
It  is  the  Platonic  School  of  the  seventeenth  century,  often  men-
tioned in  the  history  of  philosophy ;  Cudworth  and  More,  in  order  to
oppose  Atheism,  revived  the  Platonic  doctrine  of  Ideas,  which  are  the
essence  of  things,  alone  make  all  knowledge  possible,  and  presuppose
a  divine  thinking  Being.  They  assumed  a  divine  nature  in  man,
which  is  prepared  by  philosophy  to  receive  revelation.  Within  the
boundaries  of  the  faith  they  were  unusually  tolerant.  While  they  held
fast  to  Episcopacy  in  the  constitution  and  the  liturgy,  they  believed
in  the  possibility  of  tolerating  other  views  and  forms, — which  fact
drew  on  them  the  name  of  Latitudinarians.  They  formed  an  oppo-
sition inside  the  Anglican  Church  against  the  severity  of  her  rule  and
the  exclusive  laws,  which  were  passed  to  her  advantage.  To  this
School  Burnet  allied  himself:  in  his  narrative  in  particular  one  recog-
nises the  union  of  philosophic  views  with  a  peculiar  party  attitude  in
Church  and  State.

With  regard  to  the  internal  questions  of  an  ecclesiastical  nature,  which
agitated  England  and  Scotland  at  this  time,  Burnet  accordingly  took
his  standpoint  between  the  two  parties  ;  he  was  neither  for  the  Presby-
terian constitution  of  a  general  assembly,  nor  yet  for  the  re-establish-
ment of  the  Episcopate  in  the  old  sense.  Among  the  newly-appointed
Bishops  in  Scotland  there  was  one,  Leighton  of  Dunblane,  afterwards
Archbishop  of  Glasgow,  who  owing  to  a  stay  in  the  Spanish  Nether-
lands had  become  connected  with  the  Jansenists,  and  had  imbibed
something  of  their  tendency  to  deeper  and  at  the  same  time  more
practical  piety :  he  himself  was  a  kind  of  ascetic,  who  did  not  allow
himself  the  title  of  Lord,  shared  his  income  with  the  poor,  and  once
wished  to  give  up  his  bishopric,  because  he  would  not  even  have  the
appearance  of  taking  part  in  the  persecution  to  which  the  episcopal
system  was  instrumental.  But  King  Charles  II  held  him  fast.  For
this  Prince  had  already  turned  his  back  on  the  severe  form  of
Episcopacy :  after  the  fall  of  the  Chancellor  Clarendon,  and  under  the

BURNET S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 49

influence  of  Buckingham,  who  everywhere  tried  to  remove  the  sup-
porters of  the  fallen  minister,  the  government,  in  the  hope  of  thereby
acquiring  complete  authority  over  the  Church,  favoured  the  Presby-
terians again,  guaranteed  them  a  partial  indulgence,  and  approved  the
attempt  at  a  reconciliation  between  the  two  great  parties,  to  which
Leighton  devoted  himself.

Then  for  the  first  time  Burnet  took  part  in  public  life.  Already  in
his  first  office,  as  pastor  of  Saltoun,  a  position  which  he  owed  to  the
patron's  friendship  with  his  father,  he  had  lifted  up  his  voice  against
the  abuses  of  the  new  Church  authority,  especially  the  persecution,
which  was  then  in  full  swing:  in  the  year  1669  he  was,  without  effort
of  his  own  (as  he  maintains)  and  by  free  election  of  the  University,
nominated  professor  in  Glasgow.  He  fulfilled  his  office,  as  it  is  said
in  his  Life,  with  the  unwearied  zeal  of  a  schoolmaster ;  but  at  the  same
time  he  lived  and  moved  in  ecclesiastical  affairs  in  accordance  with
the  views  of  Leighton,  which  were  also  the  views  of  the  government
of  that  time.  A  more  zealous  spokesman  Leighton  could  not  find
than  the  learned,  active,  energetic  young  professor.  Burnet  was  one
of  those  whom  Leighton  sent  out  into  the  diocese,  to  spread  his
ideas  and  win  them  a  reception.  But  the  chief  object  was  to  bring
about  an  approximation  of  Episcopacy  to  the  demands  of  the  Presby-
terians. The  bishops  were  in  fact  to  be  mere  moderators  or  presi-
dents of  the  Presbyterian  assemblies.  Various  meetings  were  held  on
the  subject,  at  which  Burnet  was  specially  active.  But  the  contra-
diction between  the  two  principles  was  too  great;  it  was  the  per-
petual opposition  between  authority  rising  up  from  below  and  royal
authority  working  from  above ;  at  last  the  Presbyterians  rejected  the
whole  thing ;  and  certainly  the  question  might  have  been  raised,
whether  the  Anglican  Church  would  not  have  likewise  rejected  the
agreement,  about  which  they  were  treating.

The  most  powerful  man  in  Scotland  at  that  time  was  the  Duke  of
Lauderdale,  one  of  those  ministers  of  Charles  II,  who  are  collectively
denoted  by  the  word  Cabal ;  he  likewise  was  for  a  reconciliation  of
the  two  parties,  and  with  him  also  Burnet,  who  had  been  sent  to  him
by  his  father,  stood  in  relations  of  mutual  confidence.  But  Lauderdale,
though  an  old  Presbyterian,  was  not  devoted  to  ecclesiastical  interests  ;
it  was  his  object  above  all  things  to  make  the  King's  prerogative  sure,
to  take  part  in  the  exercise  of  the  enlarged  power  in  England,  and
with  regard  to  Scotland  to  get  it  entirely  into  his  own  hands.  He
hated  the  Presbyterians,  because  they  had  not  accepted  the  offers
made  to  them,  and  he  inclined  once  more  to  the  side  of  Episcopacy
as  it  then  existed.  It  came  to  this,  that  in  the  second  Dutch  war
leanings  of  the  Scottish  Puritans  to  the  Dutch  came  to  light,  which

RANKE,  VOL.  VI.  E

5o BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

seemed  to  justify  every  sort  of  repression ;  in  consequence  of  which
the  old  kind  of  violence  revived  again.  His  friendship  with .  Burnet
could  not  now  last  much  longer.  But  besides  this,  Lauderdale  sought
to  direct  the  Parliament  of  Scotland  by  his  command ;  hereupon  the
old  party  feuds  awoke  once  more  ;  the  Hamiltons  set  themselves
against  the  aggressive  minister;  and  Burnet  was  united  with  them.
From  the  papers,  which  the  Duchess  gave  him,  he  compiled  just  at
that  time  the  memoirs  of  the  Hamiltons,  which  are  of  great  value
owing  to  their  contents  being  original  material,  but  mark  him  as  an
adherent  of  this  House.  An  alienation  took  place  between  Burnet
and  Lauderdale,  which  had  a  decisive  effect  on  Burnet's  life.  Re-
pulsed by  the  proud  minister,  he  commenced  a  course  of  action,  which
no  one  can  excuse,  and  for  which  he  even  blames  himself  in  his  His-
tory. Always  violent  and  easily  roused,  Lauderdale  had  allowed  him-
self to  say,  in  conversation  with  Burnet,  that  he  should  be  very  glad
if  a  rebellion  broke  out  in  Scotland,  for  it  could  be  extinguished  with-
out trouble,  perhaps  with  the  help  of  the  Irish,  and  so  they  would  at
once  become  masters  of  the  country.  Another  time  he  had  even
hinted  that  they  might  wish  to  make  use  of  the  Scots,  in  order  to  crush
the  resistance  in  England.  Burnet  gave  information  of  this  to  the
minister's  enemies,  whose  object  it  then  was  to  impeach  him  in
the  English  Parliament.  He  himself  made  a  declaration  on  the  sub-
ject in  Parliament  to  the  detriment  of  his  old  patron  ;  so  thit  the
House  demanded — in  vain,  it  is  true — the  dismissal  of  the  minister  by
the  King.  Burnet  had  dedicated  one  of  his  writings  on  Church  poli-
tics to  the  minister;  he  caused  the  still  unsold  copies  to  be  recalled
from  the  bookseller's,  and  tore  out  the  dedication.  Still  Lauderdale
continued  to  be  all-powerful  in  Scotland  :  after  these  proceedings,
Burnet  did  not  venture  to  go  back  again  to  Glasgow  to  exercise  his
professorship. He  lived  henceforth  in  England.

It  was  a  small  and  subordinate,  almost  private  position,  which  en-
abled him  to  live  in  London.  He  was  chaplain  to  the  Master  of  the
Rolls,  Harbottle  Grimstone,  one  of  the  old  parliamentary  leaders,  who
had  thrown  in  his  lot  certainly  with  the  Restoration,  but  had  held  fast
the  principles  to  which  Burnet  also  did  homage.  In  London  Burnet
further  developed  his  opinions.  He  there  had  opportunity  of  making
the  acquaintance  of  the  chief  members  of  the  Cambridge  school,  whose
principles  were  his  also ;  men  like  the  circumspect  Tillotson,  the  proud,
learned  Stillingfleet,  the  severe  Patrick,  and  the  unweariedly  laborious
Tennison ; — they  were  to  this  extent  all  of  his  opinion,  in  that  they
saw  nothing  absolutely  divine  and  unalterable  in  the  constitution  of
the  Church,  and  at  the  same  time  devoted  themselves  with  the  greatest
zeal  to  preaching. But  to  begin  with,  public  attention  in  England

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 51

was  at  that  time  not  directed  to  those  differences  between  Episcopacy
'and  Presbyterianism. What  occupied  men's  minds  was  rather  the
general  anxiety  lest  the  predominance  which  Catholicism  obtained  on
the  continent  should  re-act  on  Great  Britain  through  the  heir  to  the
throne,  who  had  gone  over  to  that  faith,  should  destroy  Protestantism,
and  moreover  by  so  doing,  destroy  the  whole  civil  Constitution,  which
was bound up with  it in the closest  possible way. Burnet and
his  friends  had  attempted  to  win  over  to  themselves  the  Duke  of  York,
whose  antipathies  were  directed  against  the  claims  of  the  episcopal
Church,  which  they  also  opposed. They  soon  convinced  themselves
that  nothing  was  to  be  done  with  him,  and  that  the  danger  for  Pro-
testantism was  very  real  and  very  imminent. Forgetting  their  internal
differences,  they  flung  themselves  with  the  greatest  zeal  into  the  con-
troversy between  Papacy  and  Protestantism  ;  Tillotson  and  Tennison
in  particular  won  for  themselves  the  credit  of  confirming  the  popula-
tion of  London  in  their  faith. Under  this  influence,  Burnet  wrote  his
History  of  the  Reformation,  from  genuine,  hitherto  unknown,  docu-
ments ;  it  contributed  in  the  most  powerful  way  to  spread  the  anti-
papal  spirit  in  England. No  wonder  if  he  thereby  lost  the  favour  of
the  heir  to  the  throne,  whose  best  arguments  against  evangelical  re-
form had  been  drawn  from  the  history  of  this  event  in  England,  and
rested  on  views  which  were  now  deprived  of  their  force  by  Burnet.
Still  Burnet  did  not  exactly  side  against  the  Duke. On  the  occasion
of  the  Popish  Plot  he  expressed  the  opinion,  that  the  charges  brought
against  him  were  for  the  most  part  invented. Then  when  the  Exclu-
sion Bill  followed,  making  the  succession  of  the  Duke  of  York  doubt-
ful, he  took  up  a  position  of  mediation. He  narrates,  that  at  first  he
had  used  his  credit  with  Members  of  Parliament,  to  get  the  right  of
inheritance  recognised,  but  when  he  saw  that  that  was  impossible,
he had  endeavoured  to  induce Halifax  to  desist  from  his  violent
opposition to the exclusion; he  feared  that  it  might  come to  an
open  breach  on  the  question. So also his  Latitudinarian friends.
Shaftesbury's  ideas,  the  promotion  of  Monmouth's  interests,  were  far
from  their  minds. They  preferred  to  hold  to  King  Charles,  who  took
up  a  neutral  position  between  the  two  parties. Burnet  admired  Lord
William  Russell,  whom  he  prepared  for  death ;  but  he  did  not  agree
with  him  in  maintaining  that  the  people  had  a  right  to  open  resist-
ance, to  which  he  endeavoured  to  show  them  the  way. In  the  oppo-
sing efforts  of  parties,  he  purposely  kept  himself  from  any  intimacy
with  one  or  the  other ;  for  to  share  knowledge  without  betraying  it
was  accounted  as  a  great  crime ;  Burnet  would  not  have  been  able  to
justify  such  a  proceeding  even  to  himself. According  to  his  view
the  matter  had  not  yet  come  to  such  a  pitch  as  to  justify  resistance,  so

E  2

52 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

he  would  have  considered  it  wrong  not  to  denounce  a  plan  concerted
for  this  object,  if  it  had  become  known  to  him.

But  when  James  II  came  to  the  throne,  the  personal  position  of  the
author  altered  no  less  than  the  general  position  of  affairs.

Shortly  before  this,  on  the  anniversary  of  the  Gunpowder  Plot
(Nov.  5,  1684),  Burnet  had  preached  an  anti-papal  sermon  in  the
Rolls'  Chapel,  not  without  anxiety,  but  at  the  express  wish  of  the  old
master,  who  wished  to  give  a  proof  of  his  continued  anti-papal  senti-
ments. He  took  for  his  text  the  words,  '  Save  me  from  the  lion's
mouth/  which  he  applied  to  the  danger  awaiting  Protestants  of  being
annihilated  by  the  Catholics ;  in  it  he  mentioned  the  wish  once  uttered
by  James  I,  that  none  of  his  family  might  ever  undertake  the  introduc-
tion of  popery.  This  of  course  made  the  very  worst  impression  on  the
quite  undoubtedly  Catholic  heir  apparent,  who  already  at  that  time  was
exercising  a  powerful  influence.  He  considered  himself  all  the  more  in-
jured inasmuch  as  he  knew  Burnet  personally.  The  doctor,  who  in  other
ecclesiastical  differences  had  felt  the  influence  of  the  Duke  to  his  cost,
lost  his  place  with  the  Master  of  the  Rolls ;  he  soon  had  reason  also  to
fear  the  disfavour  of  the  new  government,  which  came  into  office
immediately  afterwards.  King  James  refused  him  the  audience  for
which  he  asked.  On  that  there  came,  as  he  says,  a  still  further  con-
sideration. He  saw  the  preparations  being  made  for  a  rebellion,
which  he  did  not  hold  to  be  justified;  he  even  maintains  that  he
warned  his  friends  from  taking  any  part  in  it.  But  he  was  just  as
little  willing  to  stand  on  the  side  of  a  government  which  followed  a
Catholicising  tendency  abominable  to  him.  Under  these  circumstances
he  thought  it  most  advisable  to  leave  England  and  resume  his  travels
on  the  continent.  He  had  no  presentiment,  and  could  have  none,  of
the  position  which  he  would  attain  in  his  voluntary  exile;  a  more
influential  one  by  far  than  any  which  could  have  fallen  to  his  lot  in  the
usual  way.

Before  we  come  to  it,  let  us  halt  awhile  over  his  historical  work,  so
far  as  it  relates  to  the  earlier  years  of  a  life  which  even  then  had
already  been  full  of  action.

An  actual  history  of  the  time  it  is  not :  Burnet  himself  says,  that  he
purposely  does  not  enter  into  circumstances  which  are  to  be  found  in
extant  histories ; — he  is  perhaps  even  wanting  in  power  to  grasp  the
internal  connexion  of  the  events.  An  important  tendency  of  the  Stuart
kings,  such  as  was  certainly  peculiar  to  later  ones,  though  not  to  the
earlier,  was  sufficient  in  his  eyes  to  explain  their  policy ;  but  if  I
may  venture  to  say  so,  it  remained  a  mystery  to  him  why  the  govern-
ment for  a  time  favoured  his  idea  of  an  accommodation  in  Scotland
and  opened  the  way  for  his  first  efforts. Of  Charles  IPs  relation  to

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 53

France,  which,  as  it  varied  from  time  to  time,  determined  the  course
of  everything,  and  even  of  the  opposition,  he  had  no  notion.

This  is,  however,  often  the  defect  of  contemporary  authors,  who
do  not  stand  at  the  centre  of  affairs.  The  really  influential  motives
remain  concealed  from  them,  and  they  endeavour  to  explain  events  by
conjectures  current  at  the  time  and  stated  in  conversation  as  facts.

In  the  introductory  narrative  down  to  the  Restoration  Burnet  enters
only  slightly  into  the  development  of  affairs,  because  that  was  suffi-
ciently well  known  from  Clarendon ;  he  merely  adds  what  he  had
heard  from  his  father,  his  uncle,  or  through  other  family  traditions,
which  go  back  even  to  his  great-grandmother,  and  from  Lauderdale,  so
long  as  he  was  his  friend,  the  Presbyterian  Lord  Hollis,  or  again  from
a  German  friend  called  Fabricius,  from  Colonel  Titus,  whose  authority
was  Charles  II  himself;  information  at  second  and  third  hand,  the
authenticity  of  which  is  not  increased  by  the  fact  that  he  gives  the  names
of  his  authorities;  for  these  themselves  had  no  sufficient  knowledge.
Burnet  has  allowed  himself  to  say  altogether  incredible  things ;  e.g.
that  Buckingham  was  induced  by  the  promise  that  he  should  be
allowed  to  come  once  more  to  France,  to  carry  on  a  mere  sham  war
for  the  rescue  of  Rochelle,  or  that  Charles  I  promised  the  Scots  to
unite  the  Northern  counties  with  Scotland,  and  make  Newcastle  the
centre  of  the  enlarged  kingdom.  That  Charles  II  had  already  gone
over  to  Catholicism  at  the  time  of  his  exile  he  believes  on  the  strength
of  the  statement  of  a  preacher,  who  had  it  from  a  Protestant  magnate,
this  last  having  also  been  solicited  to  go  over  to  Catholicism  by  the
Cardinal  (Mazarin).

This  style  and  manner  finds  its  way  into  the  actual  History  also ;
but  here  we  meet  at  the  same  time  a  special  knowledge  of  facts,  which
deserves  attention.

One  can  divide  the  matter  into  two ;  contemporaneous  circum-
stances, of  which  Burnet  as  a  contemporary  had  a  more  or  less  exact
knowledge ;  and  reports  of  his  own  immediate  experiences.

In  the  first  the  attitude  of  mediation,  which  he  had  in  general  taken,
stood  him  in  good  stead ;  his  narratives  here  are  for  the  most  part
impartial.  Into  the  sharp  opposition  between  the  Whigs  and  Tories,
which  became  prominent  in  the  last  years  of  Charles  II,  he  enters  little
or  not  at  all,  either  in  his  politics  or  in  his  narrative.  The  arguments,
which  each  side  brought  forward  on  its  own  behalf,  he  places  honestly
together  and  contrasts  them.  Bitter  foe  as  he  was  of  the  Jesuits,  yet
