he  speaks  with  abhorrence  of  the  proceedings  of  their  accusers.  His
statements  do  not  throw  complete  light  on  the  events,  but  still  they
are  always  very  noteworthy  and  instructive.

The  chief  value  of  the  work  lies  in  the  narration  of  the  affairs,  in

54 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

which  Burnet  himself  had  taken  part.  His  account  of  the  .  attempt
at  accommodation  in  Scotland  has  been  rightly  adopted  as  historical ;
it  is  instructive  and  simple.  Very  acceptable  are  the  sketches  of  the
persons  engaged  in  it,  e.g.  Archbishop  Leighton,  which  is  drawn  with
great  affection,  as  also  of  other  Latitudinarian  friends,  who  possessed
his  sympathy.  So  also  in  the  rest  of  the  History.  Burnet's  account
of  the  Popish  Plot  deserves,  as  has  been  mentioned,  especially  to  be
read ;  it  has  peculiar  value  for  this  reason,  that  the  author  once  or
twice  spoke  with  King  Charles,  whose  opinion  appears  here  pretty
much  the  same  as  we  know  it  from  other  authentic  accounts,  but
still  with  variations,  which  are  not  found  elsewhere.  So  all  that  Burnet
says  about  his  relations  to  the  Duke  of  York,  to  whom  he  once  stood
so  near,  that  the  Duke  wished  to  place  the  editing  of  his  own  memoirs
in  his  hands,  bears  the  stamp  of  authenticity  and  truthfulness.

Burnet's  History  of  his  Own  Times  is  above  all  things  a  noting  of
what  was  memorable  in  his  own  life.  It  is  a  strange  mixture  of
rumour  and  error  with  knowledge  and  truth,  of  credulous  partiality
and  the  effort  to  be  impartial; — subjective  truthfulness  one  cannot
exactly  dispute  in  our  author;  but  the  objective  truth  of  the  facts
which  he  handles  one  must  often  deny.

This  is  especially  the  case  in  his  account  of  the  reign  of  James  II,
of  which,  being  out  of  England,  he  was  not  an  eyewitness,  and
only  knew  the  events  by  report  at  second-hand,  as  they  were
spread  about  in  all  the  world  by  James'  enemies.  He  too  belonged
to  the  malcontents,  and  was  regarded  as  such  after  his  removal  from
England ;  for  up  to  that  time  his  position  had  not  been  so  sharply
defined.  All  that  was  said  against  the  King  and  his  party,  the
Camarilla,  Burnet  heard  at  a  distance  and  put  into  his  book.  His
narrative  becomes  more  untrustworthy  and  partial  in  proportion  as
the  events  gain  in  importance.  One  can  scarcely  read  anything  more
improbable  than  Burnet's  account  of  the  birth  of  the  Prince  of  Wales,
whom  he  declares  absolutely  to  be  supposititious.

Burnet  has,  for  instance,  allowed  himself  to  state  more  than
once  that  the  mother-in-law  of  King  James,  the  old  Duchess  of
Modena,  had  made  a  vow  in  case  her  daughter,  the  Queen  of  England,
should  bring  a  son  into  the  world,  and  that  on  the  6th  of  October,
on  which  day  the  child  was  said  to  have  been  conceived,  although  the
Duchess  was  already  dead  in  July.  He  lays  stress  on  the  fact  that
the  accoucheur  Chamberlain  was  not  summoned  at  the  right  time ;  but
we  have  this  man's  letter,  in  which  he  says  that  the  Court  sent  for
him,  but  that  the  messenger  chanced  not  to  find  him  at  home.  If  an
imposture  had  been  intended,  Chamberlain  would  certainly  not  have
been  summoned ;  he  was  known  as  a  Whig. Burnet  states  that  besides

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 55

the  main  entrance  there  was  another  entrance  into  the  Queen's
chamber.  And  so  there  was ;  but  we  know  from  Mackenzie,  a  witness
not  open  to  suspicion,  that  a  large  wardrobe,  difficult  to  move,  was
placed  in  front  of  this  door.  Burnet  also  has  the  story  of  the  warming-
pan,  in  which  it  was  said  that  the  child  was  introduced :  one  finds
everything  in  him  that  can  strengthen  suspicion,  just  as  it  was  told  at
the  Hague  at  the  time,  however  improbable  it  might  be.  He  was
generally  credulous  and  uncritical.  How  could  he  fail  to  be  still  more
so  than  usual  in  this  all-important  party-question  ?

Although  we  are  obliged  in  this  as  in  so  many  points  to  set  aside
Burnet's  report  of  what  took  place  in  England,  yet  on  the  other
hand  his  account  of  his  stay  at  the  Hague  is  invaluable.  He  won  the
most  intimate  confidence  of  the  Prince  and  Princess,  especially  of  the
Princess,  who  held  fast  to  the  Anglican  Church,  not,  however,  without
cherishing  Latitudinarian  sympathies.  Specially  characteristic  are  the
conferences  which  Burnet  used  to  have  with  her,  and  which  he  has
described  in  detail.  Burnet's  report  of  the  preparations  of  the  Prince
of  Orange  for  his  English  expedition  is  by  no  means  entirely  sufficient,
but  still  it  is  the  best  that  we  have  left  from  the  period  itself.  It  was
the  chief  event  of  his  life  that  he  was  able  himself  to  contribute  towards
it :  the  two  great  tendencies  of  his  soul  were  herein  united.  The
question  was,  to  prevent  the  re-establishment  of  Catholicism,  in  which
French  and  Jesuit  interests  worked  together,  and  on  the  other  hand  to
unite  Episcopalians  and  Presbyterians.  It  was  of  no  small  importance
that  the  Prince,  zealous  Calvinist  as  he  was,  and  therefore  allied  in  creed
to  the  Presbyterians,  was  induced  to  allay  the  antipathies  which  the
Episcopalians  felt  against  him.  Burnet  was  especially  fitted  to  give
this  direction  to  English  opinion,  and  to  impart  trustworthy  infor-
mation respecting  the  views  of  the  Prince  as  answering  to  what  was
desired.

One  question  only  arises  about  this,  viz.  :  how  Burnet,  once  a  warm
champion  of  royal  authority,  who  rejected  the  Covenant  because  the
right  of  resistance  was  maintained  in  it,  how  this  same  man  now
brought  himself  to  encourage  the  Prince  and  Princess  in  an  under-
taking which  was  based  on  the  supposition  that  all  England  would
rise  in  armed  resistance  against  King  James.

It  is  a  question  which  is  discussed  in  detail  in  the  great  code  of
public  law,  which  at  that  time  enjoyed  universal  authority,  Hugo  Grotius
de  jure  belli  et  pacis.  In  it  there  is  a  special  chapter  De  subditorum
bello  in  superiores.  Not  to  resist  is  held  by  Grotius  also  as  in
general  a  religious  duty.  The  position  of  the  Scottish  reformers,  that
the  early  Christians  did  not  resist  the  Roman  emperors  merely  because
they  were too  weak  to do so,  he rejects expressly,  alleging  from

56 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

Tertullian  that  they  would  have  been  strong  enough  if  they  had  only
thought  it  right.  But  to  this  again  he  sets  limits,  and  then  enumerates
the  most  important  cases  in  which  resistance  is  nevertheless  allowable,
e.  g.  if  a  prince  alienates  his  kingdom  or  makes  it  dependent  on  others,
if,  under  the  guidance  of  a  wild  desire,  he  leads  his  people  to  destruc-
tion, a  point  which  William  Barclay  (a  Scot  and  in  general  a  very
religious  author,  to  whom  Grotius  often  refers)  had  already  assumed.
Grotius  lays  special  stress  on  the  cases  in  which  the  prince  is  declared
in  the  constitution  to  be  responsible,  as  in  Castile,  or  in  which  re-
sistance is  expressly  reserved  as  in  Aragon.  The  most  important  case
is,  where  the  prince  is  not  in  full  possession  of  the  supreme  power,  a
portion  having  been  reserved  to  a  senate  or  the  people ;  then  so  far
as  he  tries  to  get  possession  of  a  power  which  does  not  belong  to  him,
resistance  may  be  offered  to  him.  '  Regi  in  partem  non  suam  in-
volanti  vis  justa  opponi  potest.'  It  is  the  13th  paragraph  of  the  4th
chapter  in  the  13th  book,  and  one  of  the  most  important  in  the  work,
for  this  was  precisely  the  case  which  could  most  easily  occur  and  did
occur.

When,  therefore,  Burnet  up  to  this  time  had  been  against  resistance,
as  mentioned,  e.g.  in  the  case  of  Lord  Russell,  this  was  because  he
held  that  things  had  not  yet  gone  so  far  as  to  justify  resistance.  '  We
thought/  he  says  of  himself  and  Tillotson,  '  that  resistance  in  the  con-
dition we  were  then  in  was  not  lawful.'  (I.  557.)  Now,  however,  he
was  of  another  opinion.

In  November  1688,  appeared  a  pamphlet  by  Burnet;  'An  en-
quiry into  the  measure  of  submission  and  the  supreme  authority,
and  of  the  grounds  on  which  it  may  be  lawful  for  subjects  to  defend
their  religion  and  libertie  ; '  that  is  respecting  the  limits  of  the  supreme
power,  and  the  right  of  offering  resistance  to  it.

Like  a  man,  who  above  all  things  is  a  theologian,  he  commences  by
rebutting  the  passages  of  Scripture,  which  are  quoted  on  behalf  of
absolute  submission ;  nor  will  he  allow  himself  to  enter  upon  specula-
tive grounds ;  he  considers  the  special  laws  of  each  several  state  alone
to  be  the  criterion.

Now  in  England,  he  continues,  the  State  is  based  upon  the  distinction
between  legislative  and  executive  power, — the  former  being  divided
between  the  King  and  the  Parliament,  the  latter  possessed  by  him
alone.  No  doubt  it  is  declared  unlawful  to  take  up  arms  against  the
King  under  any  pretext  whatever ;  but  this  holds  good  only  in  re-
spect to  the  King's  executive  power,  and  therefore  in  regard  to  the
administration  ;  one  must  not  resist  the  King,  because  the  administra-
tion is  bad :  but  the  obligation  to  obedience  does  not  involve  sub-
mission to  an  invasion  of  the  legislative  power  or  the  subversion  of

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 57

the  constitution.  But  a  case  like  this  had  now  occurred  in  Eng-
land. For  what  was  left  of  legislative  power,  when  laws  were  dis-
pensed with  or  suspended,  and  that  for  all  future  time;  when  cor-
porations were  arranged  in  such  a  manner,  that  for  a  future  parliament
only  those  could  be  elected  whom  the  King  wished  ?  It  was  impos-
sible that  the  King  should  be  allowed  to  overturn  the  whole  founda-
tions of  the  constitution,  on  which  he  himself  rested ;  in  such  cases
one  could  either  depose  the  King,  or  at  any  rate  associate  with  him  a
tutor  or  guardian,  as  had  been  done  a  little  while  before  in  Portugal,
with  the. approbation  of  Charles  II  himself.

These  were  the  principles  on  which  the  Prince  of  Orange  justified
himself  when  he  came  over  to  support  the  resistance  which  had  been
prepared  in  England ;  for  thus  only  was  it  intended  to  act  in  the
matter :  before  the  revolt  which  was  springing  up  on  all  sides  King
James  then  took  to  flight.

Burnet,  who  accompanied  the  Prince,  greeted  this  circumstance,
to  which  he  had  indirectly  contributed,  with  great  satisfaction.  In
the  debate  which  followed,  he  declared  against  the  setting  up  of  a
regency,  because  in  that  case  the  runaway  King  would  always  have
retained  his  title  and  a  certain  amount  of  influence.  So  far  he  agreed
with  the  Whig  party  ;  but  not  farther.  Already  in  the  question  about
the  original  contract,  which  they  brought  into  recognition  in  the  final
decision,  he  held  himself  indifferent ;  he  was  not  against  it,  but  neither
was  he  for  it ;  for  it  seemed  to  him  that  King  James  had  violated  not
so  much  the  dubious  right  deduced  from  the  primitive  compact  as
the  very  distinct  obligations  of  a  King  of  England.  But  he  separated
definitely  from  them,  when  the  question  as  to  who  should  now  occupy
the  throne  was  discussed.

Here  again,  as  above  in  the  case  of  Clarendon,  it  happens  that  I
have  once  more  to  mention  circumstances  already  discussed  in  general
in  the  course  of  the  narrative,  in  order  to  note  the  position  of  the
author  with  regard  to  them.

The  Whigs,  who  held  fast  to  the  theory  that  all  power  proceeds
from  the  people,  intended  now  to  give  this  theory  a  practical  ap-
plication by  the  transfer  of  the  Crown  to  William  Prince  of  Orange
alone,  without  any  consideration  of  the  nearer  heirs.  In  the  abstract
William,  who  had  a  vivid  notion  of  the  prerogative,  and  wished  it
to  be  maintained  so  far  as  it  had  a  legal  basis,  was  against  the  theory
of  the  Whigs ;  but  there  was  a  moment  in  which  those  about  him
gave  into  the  proposal.  Bentink,  who  might  be  regarded  as  the
alter  ego  of  the  Prince,  one  day  visited  Burnet  to  dispose  him
also  towards  it.  His  ground  was,  that  the  sovereign  power  could
rest  only  in  one  person ;  no  doubt  the  Princess  was  entirely  devoted

58 BURXET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

to  her  husband,  but  all  human  beings  are  weak ;  who  could  guarantee
the  future  ?  The  Queen  must  be  merely  the  King's  consort.  Against
this,  however,  Burnet, — we  know  how  near  he  stood  to  the  Princess,
— raised  a  very  energetic  opposition.

At  that  time  he  had  been  appointed  by  the  Prince  as  his  chaplain.
The  next  day  he  visited  Bentink  to  get  him  to  ask  the  Prince  to  free
him  from  this  new  position ;  it  would  prevent  him  from  opposing  the
design  communicated  to  him,  and  yet  he  had  determined  to  do  this
with  all  possible  emphasis.  Bentink  begged  him  to  wait,  as  nothing
was  as  vet  settled.  After  some  consideration  all  concurred  in  the
view,  which  was  the  dominant  one,  and  at  last  was  raised  to  be  a  re-
solution, that  William  and  Mary  should  be  King  and  Queen  of  Eng-
land, and  should  possess  the  royal  power  in  common.  Burnet,  who
had  the  surest  knowledge  that  the  Queen  would  leave  the  authority
entirely  to  her  husband,  perhaps  contributed  most  towards  setting
aside  the  opposition  which  the  other  supporters  of  the  Prince  raised
against  a  somewhat  divided  power.

Yet  here  again  new  theoretical  doubts  showed  themselves.

If  the  Tories,  in  order  to  recede  as  little  as  possible  from  the  rights
inherent  in  the  crown,  were  of  opinion  that  after  the  departure  of  the
King  his  daughter  must  be  recognised  as  Queen,  then  it  would  follow
that  William  III  was  King  only  so  far  as  his  wife  transferred  her  rights
to  him.  Against  this  William  had  declared  with  the  utmost  decision
that  he  would  wear  the  crown  in  his  own  right.  But  one  then  came
back  again  to  the  question  of  right ;  what  was  his  personal  right  ?
The  Whigs  based  it  on  the  spontaneous  right  of  the  nation  to  elect.
Burnet,  who  meanwhile  had  become  Bishop  of  Salisbury,  being  still
averse  to  this,  put  forward  another  theory  in  a  pastoral  letter.  We
may  believe  him,  when  he  tells  us  that  the  invention  of  it  was  due
to  Lloyd,  Bishop  of  St.  Asaph,  one  of  the  seven  who  had  opposed
King  James ;  the  question,  however,  is  not  of  much  importance,  for
Burnet  makes  it  his  own,  and  puts  it  forth  in  public  with  his  episcopal
authority.

Lloyd  and  Burnet  supposed  that  King  William  had  acquired  a
right  of  his  own,  independent  of  the  hereditary  claim  of  his  wife,  to
the  crown,  because  it  had  fallen  to  him  .in  a  righteous  war.  For  no
one  could  deny  that  an  heir  has  the  right  to  take  care  of  his  inheri-
tance, when  it  is  being  reduced  to  ruin  by  the  possessor :  how  much
more  the  heir  of  a  crown,  when  he  sees  that  it  is  being  placed  under
a  foreign  jurisdiction,  and  thus  robbed  of  its  security  as  well  as  of  its
honour?  The  greatest  champion  of  passive  obedience  must  allow
that  a  sovereign  prince,  to  whom  this  happens,  has  the  right  to  visit
another  with  war. That  had  been  the  case  here,  and  the  war  of  the

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 59

Prince  against  the  King  had  been  undertaken  on  a  rightful  ground.
But  it  was  an  undoubted  principle  of  right,  recognised  by  all  lawyers,
that  the  success  of  a  rightful  war  gave  a  rightful  claim  to  all  that  was
won  in  the  course  of  the  war.  The  Prince  of  Orange  might  have
caused  himself  to  be  proclaimed  King  at  once  :  he  had,  however,  left
the  decision  to  the  Lords  and  Commons  of  England.

Burnet  made  a  distinction  between  the  resolutions  of  the  conven-
tion by  which  the  prince  was  raised  to  the  throne,  and  the  divine
decision  by  the  result  of  the  rightful  war.  In  regard  to  the  nation
William  was  a  protector;  in  regard  to  James  II  the  conqueror  of  his
rights.  The  decision  of  arms  in  favour  of  the  Prince  was  a  decision
of  God,  to  which  man  must  submit.  One  thus  got  back  to  the  idea
of  divine  right  in  a  way  not  very  different  from  that  in  which  Crom-
well made  it  tell  in  his  own  favour.  It  was  said,  that  God  disposes
as  He  will  of  the  kingdom,  and  Holy  Writ  even  recognises  the  Roman
Empire,  which  in  like  manner  was  in  the  first  instance  set  up  by  force.

Historically  Burnet's  view  is  not  unfounded;  for  it  is  clear  that
the  Prince  of  Orange  had  already  got  the  supreme  power  into  his
hands  before  any  one  surrendered  it  to  him,  by  the  course  of  events,
and  by  his  victory,  bloodless  as  it  was.

We  leave  it  to  others  to  investigate  whether  this  view  was  tenable
legally  or  theologically.  Burnet  assures  us  that  it  contributed  much
towards  inducing  the  church  and  the  country  to  submit.  The  Angli-
can clergy  could  submit  to  the  King  more  easily,  in  so  far  as  he  had
come  to  the  throne  by  the  issue  of  circumstances,  in  which  people
saw  the  will  of  God,  than  if  his  right  had  been  deduced  from  a
decree  of  the  Parliament.

But  obviously  the  whole  view  ran  counter  to  parliamentary  ideas ;
on  the  side  of  the  Whigs  it  aroused  the  most  violent  opposition.

The  Whigs  deduced  the  right  of  the  Prince  to  invade  England  from
the  invitation  of  the  country,  which  had  been  sent  to  him,  not  formally
it  is  true,  but  unmistakeably  ;  and  his  right  to  reign  from  the  resolutions
of  the  Convention  and  from  the  Settlement.  They  thought  by  this
means  to  see  their  doctrine  of  the  sovereignty  of  the  people,  and  of
government  being  founded  on  compact,  realised.  That  the  Princess
had  been  recognised  at  the  same  time  seemed  to  them  to  be  an  un-
essential concession.  But  to  ascribe  to  the  Prince  such  a  thing  as
a  divine  right,  they  held  to  be  an  affront  to  the  nation  and  a  violation
of  the  Constitution.  Burnet  had  the  bitter  mortification  of  having  his
pastoral  letter  condemned  by  the  Lower  House  to  be  burnt  by  the
hangsman.  The  Upper  House  would  not  go  so  far ;  but  it  declared
on  its  side  also,  that  the  view  was  in  contradiction  to  the  principles
of  the  Constitution.

60 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

In  the  year  1699,  Burnet  was  nominated  to  be  tutor  to  the  Duke
of  Gloucester,  at  that  time  heir  presumptive,  an  office  to  which  he
devoted  himself  with  the  application  of  a  born  teacher.  In  the  Lower
House  of  Parliament  he  experienced  many  attacks  on  the  subject ;  the
Whigs  reproached  him  with  the  above-mentioned  theories  of  divine
right ;  they  thought  that  a  man  of  such  principles  ought  not  to  be
admitted  to  this  office.  But  the  Tories,  and  especially  the  supporters
of  the  Princess  Anne,  kept  always  in  remembrance  his  attitude  with
regard  to  hereditary  right ;  they  did  not  wish  to  see  a  champion  of
national  sovereignty  holding  such  a  post.  He  retained  his  place;
without  results,  however ;  for  the  boy,  who  had  already  excited  much
attention,  soon  after  died.

But  at  this  time  an  opposition  was  raised  against  Burnet  from
another  side,  and  was  to  affect  him  still  more  deeply.

The  leading  thought  of  his  life  was  the  reconciliation  of  the  two
ecclesiastical  forms,  the  Anglican  and  the  Presbyterian;  and'the  most
necessary  prerequisite  was  an  abatement  of  the  exclu^ve  rights  of
the  former.  This  was  precisely  the  idea  of  the  Latitudinarians,
who  also  had  allied  themselves  with  William  III.  To  this  extent
the  Platonists  of  Cambridge,  by  whom  these  views  were  promoted,
exercised  a  great  influence  on  the  crisis  of  the  Constitution  and
the  history  of  England  generally.  When  the  strong  Anglicans  re-
fused the  oath  to  the  new  government,  the  Latitudinarians  stepped
into  their  place.  It  was  an  incalculable  advantage  to  William  III
that  he  found  for  the  archiepiscopal  see  of  Canterbury  a  man  like
Tillotson,  who  enjoyed  universal  respect  and  deserved  it.  In  a  short
time  fifteen  episcopal  sees  became  vacant,  which  were  all  filled  up
with  men  of  the  same  way  of  thinking :  one  of  these  was  our  Burnet,
to  whom  was  committed  the  great  diocese  of  Salisbury.

They  were  not  able  to  carry  out  their  leading  idea ;  they  were
obliged  to  content  themselves  with  simple  tolerance  of  the  Dissenters
without  political  rights ;  they  exercised  their  office  in  a  spirit  of  the
greatest  forbearance  and  consideration.  In  this  they  were  entirely  at
one  with  the  King,  whose  authority  became  very  effective  through
close  union  with  the  bishops.

But  it  was  precisely  this  authority,  exercised  by  the  crown  through
the  bishops,  which  excited  an  opposition  in  the  episcopal  church  itself.

Hitherto  the  King's  supremacy  and  the  spiritual  power  inherent  in
the  bishops  had  been  one  of  the  main  principles  on  which  the  oppo-
sition to  the  Papacy  rested.  But  seeing  that  former  bishops  had
always  maintained  and  put  into  practice  the  idea  of  church  independ-
ence, even  with  regard  to  the  crown,  now  that  on  the  contrary  the
bishops  held  unconditionally  to  the  government,  church opposition

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 61

descended  to  lower  circles :  it  took  up  its  position  in  the  Lower  House
of  Convocation.

The  summoning  of  Convocation  had  been  for  a  long  time  inter-
mitted, and  was  first  demanded  by  zealous  ecclesiastical  writers,  such
as  Dr.  Atterbury.  When  the  King  in  the  year  1700  saw  himself  com-
pelled to  fall  back  on  the  Tory  ministers,  and  the  elections  resulted  in
a  Tory  Parliament,  he  was  compelled  to  allow  Convocation  also  to
meet;  this  took  place  in  February  1701.

The  very  first  sittings  were  exceedingly  stormy.  The  Lower  House
of  Convocation  claimed  rights  in  spiritual  matters  similar  to  those  of
the  Commons  in  temporal.  And  just  as  at  that  time  it  not  unfre-
quently  came  to  violent  quarrels  between  Lords  and  Commons,  so
the  Lower  House  of  Convocation  set  itself  in  opposition  to  the
bishops.  Against  their  will  it  assumed  the  right  of  pronouncing  a
judgment  on  theological  writings.  One  of  the  books  which  fell
under  their  censure  was  Burnet's  Exposition  of  the  Thirty-nine
Articles,  a  work  that  in  the  main  may  be  regarded  as  a  product  of
Latitudinarian  opinion ;  it  admitted  a  variety  of  views,  which  the
zealous  churchmen  would  not  allow.

So  long  as  King  William  lived,  however,  and  the  commission  lasted,
which  he  entrusted  with  the  conduct  of  ecclesiastical  affairs,  all  this
had  not  much  significance.

We  have  noticed  how  powerfully  the  Anglican  spirit  was  roused  at
the  accession  of  Queen  Anne,  in  whom  hereditary  right  and  church
feeling  were  united;  the  Lower  House  of  Convocation  acted  in  the
fullest  agreement  with  the  Lower  House  of  Parliament.  The  Bill
against  occasional  conformity  was  at  the  same  time  an  act  of  hostility
to  the  bishops,  who  had  connived  at  this  anomaly.  Burnet  had  done
a  great  service  to  the  Anglican  clergy ;  for  from  him  came  the  pro-
posal to  devote  the  produce  of  the  first  fruits  and  tenths,  which
formed  part  of  the  income  of  the  crown,  to  the  poor  clergy;  a
measure,  with  the  adoption  of  which  Queen  Anne  celebrated  her
birthday  in  the  year  1704.  But  that  could  not  protect  him  from  the
attacks  of  Convocation.  Nevertheless  the  Queen  still  held  to  the
bishops,  who  for  the  first  time  in  this  conflict  sided  with  the  Whigs.
Convocation  could  not  at  that  time  attain  any  regular  and  permanent
influence.

To  this  time  belongs  a  small  paper  by  Burnet,  in  which  he  endea-
vours to  give  the  Electress  Sophia  an  idea  of  the  English  constitution
and  of  English  affairs :  '  A  memorial,  humbly  offered  to  H.R.H.  the
Princess  Sophia,  Electress  and  Dutchess  of  Hanover/  dated  Lambeth,
May  15th,  O.S.  1703;  it  was  printed  in  1815  in  Hanover,  where
the  MS.  had  been  preserved.

62 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

One  would  be  deceived  if  one  were  to  expect  therein  a  picture
of  the  state  of  parties,  in  the  form  which  they  assumed  at  the  opening
of  Queen  Anne's  reign;  of  the  prominent  personages  and  their
controversies  at  the  time  next  to  nothing  whatever  is  said;  the  paper
has,  on  the  whole,  no  importance  with  regard  to  the  crisis  of  that
time.  It  is  calmly  written  information  for  the  future  queen  respect-
ing the  constitution  in  general,  peers,  commons,  and  the  crown.
Burnet  speaks  like  a  well-wishing  friend  of  the  House  of  Hanover.
He  would  be  for  a  restoration  of  the  property  of  the  crown,  including
what  belonged  to  the  Prince  of  Wales,  and  he  states  how  this  end
might  be  attained.  The  chief  means  he  sees  above  all  in  the  setting
up  of  a  popular  ministry ;  which  would  influence  Parliament  to  make
a  rich  provision  for  the  crown ;  '  to  grant  a  plentifull  revenue  to  Y.H.
as  our  souverain,  and  to  the  princes,  your  sons.'

So  he  wishes  to  see  the  nobility  also  restored  to  their  old  fortunes,
for  without  Lords  England  could  not  certainly  continue  to  exist ;
that  the  Long  Parliament  had  wished  to  do  away  with  them  seemed
to  him  to  be  madness.  The  Anglican  Church  he  declares  to  be  the
most  orthodox  and  best  ordered  church  in  the  world ;  he  sees  nothing
wanting  in  her  but  steadfast  moderation;  a  slight  abatement  in
things,  which  no  one  could  declare  to  be  essential,  would  enable  the
Presbyterians  and  even  the  Independents  to  join  the  Church.

In  the  union  with  Scotland  Burnet  took  the  most  active  part ;  he
was  president  of  the  committee  of  the  Upper  House  for  this  matter.
It  may  be  regarded  as  another  expression  of  the  Latitudinarian
feeling  of  the  Bishops,  that  the  Scottish  Church  was  allowed  to
be  equally  orthodox  with  the  English.  But  Burnet's  original  idea
was  not  realised.  For  there  was  no  longer  any  thought  of  a  recon-
ciliation and  union  of  the  two  church  forms.  He  had  to  give
up  this  ideal  of  his  youth.  The  Scots  were  allowed  to  keep  their
ecclesiastical  independence,  the  Presbyterian  form  of  their  church
was  to  continue  unchanged.

But  this  led  to  consequences,  on  which  people  had  not  reckoned.
What  was  allowed  to  the  Scottish  Church,  viz.  the  maintenance  of
their  constitution,  that  the  English  Church  also  thought  itself  bound
to  demand  for  itself  at  a  moment,  in  which  the  Legislature  was
admitting  Presbyterian  elements  into  itself:  the  old  statutes  were
renewed,  on  which  its  exclusive  authority  rested,  above  all  the  Act
of  Uniformity.  The  idea  of  church  comprehension,  to  which  the
Latitudinarians  still  held  fast,  now  of  necessity  vanished  entirely.
The  two  opposing  principles,  between  which  this  ecclesiastical  party
had  wished  to  mediate,  set  themsel/es  in  full  strength  against  one
another.

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 63

And  if  in  the  Act  of  Union  the  claim  of  the  English  Church  was
not  expressed  with  such  full  energy  as  that  of  the  Scottish,  the
sole  effect  of  this  was,  that  the  agitation  in  the  former  was  all
the  more  violent.

From  the  very  first  moment  Convocation  set  itself  against  the
Union;  and  as  it  was  feared,  that  they  would  have  recourse  to
Parliament  in  their  opposition,  it  was  thought  good  to  prorogue
Convocation.

The  political  influences,  which  we  know,  combined  with  the  eccle-
siastical .  ones ;  Burnet  himself,  like  Marlborough  and  Godolphin,
now  held  to  the  Whigs.

Then  another  sermon  was  preached  on  the  5th  of  November,  like
his  own  years  before,  which,  however,  created  still  greater  com-
motion ;  in  it  Dr.  Sacheverell  spoke  out  against  the  right  of  resistance,
and  that  in  such  a  way  that  legal  proceedings  were  instituted  against
him  by  impeachment  before  Parliament.  No  wonder,  that  this  occu-
pied public  attention  almost  exclusively  for  some  time.  For  prin-
ciples came  into  question,  on  which  the  condition  of  the  State  at
the  time,  and  of  society  rested.  Burnet  also  was  specially  concerned,
for  by  his  theory  of  the  right  of  resistance  he  had  furthered  the
Revolution.

We  are  not  now  following  the  phases  through  which  this  trial
passed.  Only  be  it  remembered,  that  it  found  an  echo  even
among  the  Lords  themselves,  when  among  others  the  Bishop  of
Bath  and  Wells  argued,  that  as  regards  the  doctrine  itself  it  might
very  well  be  correct,  but  that  it  was  dangerous  to  preach  it  to  the  people
even  if  one  limited  it  to  the  extremest  necessity.  Even  the  doctrine  of
the  original  contract  he  declared  to  be  very  questionable  ;  he  appeared
to  prefer  the  word  vacancy  or  abdication  to  the  word  revolution.

The  most  remarkable  thing  was,  that  the  great  leader  of  the  party
of  resistance  in  the  year  1688,  Danby,  who  had  himself  been  the  first  to
take  up  arms  against  James  II,  and  now  bore  the  title  of  Duke  of
Leeds,  declared  without  reserve,  that  the  object  of  that  movement
was  declared  in  the  words  abdication  and  vacancy;  had  they  not
succeeded  (so  he  seemed  to  mean),  they  would  rightly  have  been
pronounced  rebels;  the  word  resistance  must  be  passed  over  in
silence.

This,  however,  was  opposed  by  others,  who  believed  more  in  the
truth  of  the  theory,  above  all  our  author,  who  repeated  his  doctrine
about  the  extreme  case.  They  carried  the  day;  Sacheverell  was
condemned,  but  yet  only  to  a  very  mild  punishment,  and  that  out  of
respect  to  public  opinion.  The  Upper  House  might  say  what  it
liked, and even discard again the old decree of  Oxford  of  the

64 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

year  1683  in  favour  of  royal  authority;  it  is  strange  but  true;  the
doctrine  of  the  unlawfulness  of  resistance  had  at  that  time  become
popular.

In  truth  Sacheverell  had  the  upper  hand.  It  was  by  the  exhibition
of  public  feeling,  which  his  trial  produced,  that  the  Queen  was  en-
couraged to  make  the  great  change  of  ministry  in  17 10,  which  in
turn  brought  about  a  reaction  in  church  matters.

Side  by  side  with  the  Tory  Parliament  Convocation  also  entered
the  field  in  1711  with  strengthened  rights.  The  Archbishops  were
not  consulted  in  the  matter;  in  arranging  the  Quorum  all  William
Ill's  Bishops,  as  well  as  those  appointed  by  Queen  Anne,  who
had  been  on  good  terms  with  the  Whig  ministry,  were  passed  over ;
only  those  most  lately  nominated  were  included.  Atterbury  conducted
the  whole  business;  he  being  the  confidential  ally  of  Harley.  A
treatise  on  the  condition  of  religion  in  the  country,  on  the  increase  of
unbelief,  was  written  in  such  a  way,  that  the  late  government  and  the
rule  of  the  Bishops  appeared  in  a  very  doubtful  light.  The  Bishops
answered  it  with  another  pamphlet, — but  with  their  policy  of  media-
tion they  fell  daily  more  and  more  into  discredit.

When  the  Occasional  Conformity  Bill  was  again  brought  into
discussion,  they  no  longer  dared  to  oppose  it.  The  political  situa-
tion of  the  moment  rendered  it  a  matter  of  necessity  for  the  Bishops
to  give  way  on  this  point,  if  the  Whig  party  was  not  to  be  utterly
defeated.

In  his  history  Burnet  expresses  himself  calmly  and  quietly  on  the
matter ;  and  yet  the  turn  which  things  took  affected  him  personally  a
good  deal.  The  ideas,  which  he  had  defended  all  his  life,  brought
him  at  the  close  of  his  days  into  great  difficulties.  His  was  a  media-
ting nature ;  neither  Episcopalian  nor  Presbyterian,  but  a  Protestant  to
the  back-bone  ;  not  an  uncompromising  royalist,  still  less  a  republican,
but  always  moderate  and  inclined  towards  the  parliamentary  form  of
government.  He  attempted  to  work  out  this  theory  of  reconciliation
on  ecclesiastical  ground  first  of  all.  But  his  plans  were  shipwrecked
in  Scotland  at  the  outset ;  his  compromises  were  rejected  by  the
Presbyterians.  Flung  then  into  the  midst  of  the  political  struggles  in
England,  he  could  accomplish  nothing  with  either  party.  When  a
Catholic  king  ascended  the  throne,  he  thought  it  best  to  leave  the
country.  It  was  in  his  voluntary  exile,  in  which  he  associated  himself
with  the  King's  enemies,  that  he  found  for  the  first  time  a  sphere  for
his  endeavours.  To  further  these,  Presbyterians  and  Episcopalians
must  be  united.  He  found  a  means  of  recognising  hereditary
monarchy  and  yet  leaving  an  opening  for  allowing  revolt  against  it.
The  event itself  echoed  this  view,  and  gave  an  opportunity  for  its

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 65

realisation.  A  toleration,  limited  enough  no  doubt,  and  a  political
settlement  hovering  between  hereditary  right  and  parliamentary  de-
crees were  actually  established.  The  Church  party,  to  which  Burnet
belonged,  and  whose  less  rigid  doctrine  enabled  them  to  attach  them-
selves to  the  new  Prince,  who  had  ascended  the  throne  by  their  help,
won  even  a  dominant  position  in  the  Episcopal  Church  ;  and  this  they
in  their  turn  owed  to  the  Prince,  and  in  it  made  their  moderate  views
of  some  effect  between  the  two  parties.  But  not  even  so  could  Burnet
carry  his  point.  The  view  of  his  friends  and  of  his  sovereign  was  directed
not  towards  mere  toleration,  but  towards  comprehension,  that  is,
towards  such  an  ordering  of  the  doctrines  and  ceremonial  of  the
Anglican  Church,  as  that  the  Dissenters  would  be  able  to  assent  to
them.  But  the  opposition  made  by  the  Anglican  Church  was  too
strong  for  anything  to  be  accomplished  against  it.  Burnet  reckoned
on  Queen  Mary,  who  entered  into  the  idea  of  a  reconciliation  with
more  method  than  her  husband ;  but  she  died  very  early,  and  her  death
deprived  him  of  his  best  support.  His  second  political  idea,  by  means
of  which  he  thought  to  give  a  new  foundation  to  the  monarchy  of  the
Revolution,  won  no  approbation.  All  prospect  of  a  mediation  passed
away  entirely  with  the  life  of  William  III.  The  two  parties  in  the
views  and  ends  of  their  general  and  personal  politics  set  themselves
more  and  more  rudely  in  opposition  to  one  another.  Like  Marl-
borough and  Godolphin,  the  bishops  also  are  obliged  to  take  up  the
party  of  the  Whigs,  and  so  also  is  Burnet.  But  they  are  forthwith
involved  also  in  the  disasters  which  overtook  the  Whigs.  The  Lower
House  of  Convocation  is  victorious  over  the  Bench  of  the  Bishops,
where  he  played  a  great  part.  The  doctrine  of  resistance,  which  he
had  adopted — with  very  definite  qualifications,  it  is  true,  but  still  had
adopted — is  rejected  and  loses  public  favour.  In  the  frame  of  mind,
which  this  contest  and  the  turn  of  events  could  not  fail  to  produce  in
him,  he  partly  revised,  partly  wrote  the  history  of  his  own  times.  In
the  concluding  words,  which  are  a  political  admonition  to  all  classes,
as  comprehensive  as  they  are  acute,  equally  instructive  as  to  the  state
of  things  at  the  time  and  the  special  standpoint  of  the  author,  he
remarks,  that  there  are  periods  in  the  life  of  nations,  in  which  they  are
inclined  to  slavery,  but  which  are  then  followed  of  necessity  by  the  oppo-
site tendencies.  The  Whig  policy,  to  which  Burnet  attached  himself,
was  calculated  to  bring  this  about.  The  actual  succession  of  the  house
of  Hanover  seemed  to  include  everything  that  could  be  wished  and
attained.  In  the  last  years  of  his  life  Burnet  had  kept  himself  tolerably
quiet,  and  devoted  his  powers  chiefly  to  his  spiritual  calling.  Even
during  his  stay  in  London  he  rarely  passed  a  Sunday  without  preaching.
The  evening  addresses  which  he  instituted,  made  a  deep  impression
RANKE,  VOL.  VI.  F

66 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

on  those  who  heard  them,  by  their  dignity  and  earnestness.  Burnet
lived  to  see  the  arrival  of  King  George  ;  he  dedicated  the  supplement
to  his  History  of  the  Reformation,  which  appeared  just  then,  to  the
King.  He  died  soon  afterwards,  just  as  the  new  government  was
adopting  the  developed  Whig  view — March  17 15.  Under  its  regime
a  bona  fide  resuscitation  of  the  old  schemes  of  comprehension  was
certainly  not  to  be  thought  of.  But  the  essential  elements  of  Burnet's
ideas  in  church  matters  revived  under  a  more  modern  form  in  Hoad-
ley's  books ;  they  have  never  quite  perished,  and  for  his  political
views  he  left  his  historical  writings  to  posterity.
Let  us  return  once  more  to  their  objective  value.

BURNET COMPARED WITH SOME DUTCH REPORTS.

The  historical  work,  which  Burnet  left  to  the  world,  may  be  com-
pared with  Clarendon's  history,  inasmuch  as  it  has  specially  contri-
buted to  fix  men's  views  respecting  the  time.  Not  till  our  own  days
did  it  become  of  real  effect,  and  that  through  the  praise,  which  some
of  the  most  learned  authors  have  bestowed  upon  it,  and  through  the
use  which  they  have  made  of  it.

I  will  quote  an  example  :

A  certain  amount  of  impression  is  made  by  what  Mackintosh  and
Macaulay  narrate  respecting  the  refusal  of  the  Duke  of  Somerset  to
introduce  the  Nuncio  d'Adda  to  the  King.  The  Duke  had  called
attention  to  the  illegality  of  this  proceeding;  whereupon  the  King
said,  '  Don't  you  know  that  I  am  above  the  law  ? '  and  the  Duke
answered,  '  Your  majesty  is  so,  but  I  am  not.'  The  narrative  agrees
very  well  with  the  general  question  at  issue ;  it  comes  from  Burnet,  I.
7 1 7  fol.  only  with  this  difference,  that  Somerset's  answer  is  somewhat
less  pointed :  'Whatever  the  King  might  be,  himself  was  not  above  the
law.'  But  whether  this  is  true  word  for  word,  may  be  doubted.
Lonsdale  has  a  considerably  different  version.  On  the  remark  of
Somerset,  that  it  would  not  be  lawful,  the  King  replied,  that  he  would
grant  him  pardon  for  it ;  to  which  Somerset  answered  that  he  knew
that  a  pardon  was  not  valid,  if  it  was  given  to  bring  about  an  illegality;
at  which  the  King  was  much  displeased.  The  Dutch  ambassador
Citters  gives  a  detailed  account  of  the  matter  in  July  1687.  His
reports  may  be  quoted  here,  especially  as  they  elucidate  other  circum-
stances, about  which  there  was  much  discussion  at  the  time.

gelycke  gevolgen  meer.

The  story  in  Burnet  was  epigrammatically  formed  in  conversation,
and  reached  him  in  this  way.  But  the  report  of  the  ambassador
is  to  a  different  effect,  and  the  natives  follow  another  tradition.  Ac-
cording to  Barrillon  also  the  King  formed  the  idea  that  this  enactment
must  be  abolished ;  '  Les  loix  par  les  quelles  toute  communication  est
interdite  avec  le  pape ;  ce  qui  est  absurde  dans  un  royaume,  dont  le
souverain  est  catholique  romain.'

In  a  similar  way  a  great  deal  has  been  transplanted  from  Burnet ;
e.  g.  his  theory,  that  the  order  to  give  back  Magdalen  College  to  the
Protestants  was  retracted  on  news  coming  that  the  Prince's  fleet  was
delayed  by  contrary  winds ;  the  object  being  to  show,  that  the  con-
cession was  altogether  feigned.  But  in  Sancroft's  Life  (I.  346)  it  is
proved  in  detail  how  false  this  theory  is.

From  Burnet  comes  the  account  of  the  cowardice  of  James  II  at
the  battle  of  the  Boyne ;  he  states  that  the  King  kept  himself  '  at  a
safe  distance  with  his  guards ; '  but  from  Lauzun's  report  it  appears
that  he  came  vigorously  to  close  quarters.

We  do  not  mean  to  impute  it  as  a  crime  to  Burnet  that  he  gave  these
notes.  He  was  credulous  and  believed  most  easily  what  was  told  to
him  to  the  disadvantage  of  the  other  side.  Subjective  truthfulness
may  exist  in  spite  of  this,  so  far  as  it  can  be  coupled  at  all  with  party
views  and  misrepresentation.

We  cannot  say  that  he  had  completeness  and  exactness  of  descrip-
tion. Burnet's  History  of  his  Own  Times  has  received  a  continuous
criticism  from  Ralph,  as  the  History  of  the  Reformation  has  from
Collier.  In  the  latest  edition,  remarks  by  Dartmouth  and  Onslow
have  been  added,  among  which  pertinent  corrections,  some  of  them
of  historical  importance,  are  to  be  found. In  Ralph  one  sees  that

BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES. 71

Burnet  is  just  as  full  of  inaccuracies  as  Clarendon;  from  the  statements
of  the  other  two,  that  his  information  on  many  points  was  very  in-
complete.

It  is  a  chronicle  of  the  time,  in  the  main  written  from  year  to  year,
while  the  events  were  still  happening,  by  a  man  who  took  part  in
many  ways  in  those  events  and  had  personal  knowledge  of  them.  The
narrative  is  not  so  detailed  as  we  might  wish,  but  the  author's  view  is
always  worthy  of  attention.  It  does  not  make  much  matter,  if  Burnet
does  make  mistakes  in  details,  and  perhaps  dates  the  commence-
ment of  a  Parliament  wrongly ;  that  can  easily  be  corrected ;  but  it  is
of  immense  value,  that  he  gives  the  points  of  view  from  which  he  saw
things.  They  are  his  party's  points  of  view,  and  precisely  as  such  are
of  importance,  inasmuch  as  this  party  subsequently  kept  the  upper
hand.

The  autobiographical  element  obtrudes  itself  here  about  as  strongly
as  in  the  first  part  of  Clarendon ;  both  present  a  mixture  of  memoir
and  history,  which  makes  them  pleasing.

For  the  historian,  who  wishes  for  instruction,  Burnet  is  always  of
the  greatest  weight,  where  he  speaks  of  that  which  he  has  himself
experienced,  done,  and  heard.  But  here  again  one  must  still  dis-
tinguish the  statement  of  what  he  heard  from  the  fact.

Burnet  was  not  so  remote  from  affairs  as  not  to  hear  of  them,  but
on  the  other  hand  he  was  not  near  enough  to  attain  to  real  and  exact
knowledge.  Thus  he  received  various  accounts  of  the  negotiations
preliminary  to  the  Peace  of  Ryswick,  which  escaped  other  people.
As  to  the  first  meeting  between  Boufrlers  and  Portland,  by  whom  the
secret  transactions  of  William  with  Louis  XIV  were  opened,  he
obtained  communications  from  Portland  himself;  but  yet  what  he
says  about  it  is  only  half  true.  At  the  very  outset  he  is  incorrect  in
saying  that  it  was  Boufflers  who  invited  the  meeting :  the  position
of  William  III  is  made  obscure,  when  Burnet  denies  that  the  king
made  the  first  overtures ;  and  when  it  is  stated,  that  Louis  XIV
promised  not  only  not  to  support  King  James  but  also  to  remove  him
to  Avignon  or  Rome,  the  fact  is  that  this  was  what  the  English
proposed,  but  Louis  XIV  never  actually  promised  the  latter,  for  it
would  have  been  contrary  to  his  honour,  nor  yet  the  former  in  the
direct  way  in  which  it  is  here  stated.  The  French  appear  in  Burnet
to  a  greater  disadvantage  than  was  the  fact,  and  this  throws  a  false
light  on  all  that  follows.  Probably  Portland  only  gave  the  bishop  a
general  statement  in  the  spirit  in  which  he  wished  the  matter  to  be
regarded  in  England.  The  lines  of  approximation  were  far  more
favourable  to  France  than  appears  in  Burnet.

So  again  in  the  conditions  of  peace  between  the  French  and  the
German  Empire  the  cession  of  Straszburg  is  represented  far  too  strongly

72 BURNET'S  HISTORY  OF  HIS  OWN  TIMES.

as  an  act  of  agreement  between  the  Emperor  and  the  French ;  whereas
the  conclusion  of  the  treaty  stuck  at  the  opposition  of  the  Emperor
and  the  Germans,  and  all  the  world  was  indignant  at  the  demand  of
the  French  to  retire  from  the  alternative.  Burnet  merely  describes  the
matter  as  it  was  communicated  to  him.

He  mentions,  that  the  French  refugees  gained  nothing  by  the  treaty  :
he  had  probably  not  heard  that  William  let  their  cause  drop  in  the
negotiations  about  Orange;  whereupon  France  gave  up  the  restora-
tion of  the  Jacobites  to  England.

Burnet  was  by  no  means  agreed  with  William  III  in  each  and  every-
thing. Sometimes  he  made  representations  to  him,  which  were  by  no
means  well  received ;  but  still  he  always  depicts  him  with  great  affec-
tion ;  for  the  transactions,  which  most  redound  to  the  King's  discredit,
he  pleaded  the  excuses  which  since  his  day  have  often  been  repeated.
He  says  well,  one  must  take  him  as  God  has  given  him.  But  then
a  candid  description  of  the  acts  of  violence,  which  occurred,  might  find
a  place.

Respecting  the  Partition  Treaties  he  is  only  very  imperfectly  in-
formed. It  was  enough  for  him,  that  he  was  convinced,  that  the
interests  of  the  country  had  not  been  injured,  even  though  the  con-
stitutional form  had  not  been  observed.  He  takes  the  Whig  ministers
under  his  protection,  and  declares  without  hesitation  that  they  were
free  from  all  blame ;  whereas  the  greatest  admirers  of  Lord  Somers,
against  whom  the  principal  charge  was  directed,  admit  his  culpability.
But  in  siding  more  and  more  energetically  with  the  Whig  party,  he
becomes  unjust  towards  the  Tories.  He  accuses  the  Parliament  of
1700,  in  which  the  Tories  had  the  upper  hand  (to  which,  however,  are
due  both  the  establishment  of  the  succession  of  the  House  of  Hanover
in  England  and  the  introduction  to  the  war  of  the  Spanish  succession)
of  having  been  bribed  by  the  French  ambassador,  as  was  seen,  he
says,  from  the  flooding  of  the  country  with  French  money.  I  will  not
say  that  bribery  may  not  have  taken  place  on  this  occasion,  as  on
previous  ones;  but  the  flooding  of  the  country  with  French  gold
pieces  was  due  rather  to  the  fact  that  more  was  given  for  them  in
England  than  abroad,  as  is  shown  by  the  edict,  which  was  called  for
by  Sir  Isaac  Newton.

The  attributing  bad  motives  to  his  opponents  is  a  fundamental
feature  in  his  narrative,  especially  in  the  reign  of  Queen  Anne :  the
remarks,  which  have  been  made  from  the  Tory  side  upon  the  work,
are  mainly  directed  against  this,  and  for  the  most  part  with  good
reason.

But  I  have  now  something  further  of  a  most  surprising  character  to
say  respecting  the  effect  of  his  position  as  a  party  man  (or  was  it

BURNET'S  MS.  AND  PRINTED  TEXT  73

other  influences  bearing  upon  his  book  ?)  upon  his  mode  of  writing
history.

Differences  between  the  Manuscript  of  the  History  and  the  printed  Text.

As  I  have  already  remarked,  Burnet  wrote  his  descriptions  from
time  to  time  during  the  several  epochs  of  his  life.  In  various  places
the  words  of  the  extant  text  show  that  they  have  not  been  re-
touched :  they  bear  the  impress  of  the  moment ;  he  notices  present
circumstances,  the  existing  crisis,  that  is,  the  one  in  the  midst  of  which
he  was  writing.

Some  of  the  earlier  sections,  however,  have  been  retouched;  yet
even  of  these  the  original  draft  still  exists  to  a  certain  extent.  It  is
preserved  in  the  British  Museum,  imperfect  it  is  true,  and  in  parts  a
copy  of  the  original ;  but  yet  always  so  authentic,  that  a  comparison  of
the  printed  text  of  1724  and  1734  with  the  original  became  a  historian's
duty.

It  would  matter  little,  if  it  were  a  question  of  a  few  passages,  for-
gotten in  the  first  instance  and  inserted  afterwards ;  or  of  differences
in  the  wording,  as  a  note  by  Ellis  states,  according  to  which  the  words
indeed  are  different,  but  yet  the  sense  is  commonly  the  same ;  for  one
cannot  be  concerned  with  an  investigation  of  style,  but  with  the  con-
tents of  the  narrative.

Here,  however,  a  difference  was  apparent,  which  fairly  astonished
me.  I  compared  first  of  all  the  account  of  the  various  events  at  the
end  of  the  year  1688,  and  of  the  early  events  in  1689.

I  at  once  noticed  a  remarkable  difference  in  individual  expressions.

For  instance,  in  the  printed  text  there  is  mention  already  at  that  time
of  Whigs  and  Tories;  but  in  fact  the  parties  had  not  yet  become
fixed  in  this  fashion.  In  the  original  draft  the  opposition  which
appears  is  between  'Republicans'  and  'the  other  party.'  In  the  later
draft  it  is  said  of  the  one  party,  that  the  Whigs  by  long  opposition
and  jealousy  against  the  government  had  worked  themselves  into  re-
publican principles  and  now  were  unable  to  free  themselves  from
them ;  '  the  other  party'  appears  as  the  Tories.

Of  the  first  party,  which  had  had  the  greatest  influence  in  declaring
the  throne  vacant,  Burnet  says  in  his  first  draft,  that  they  had  ex-
cited anxiety  in  the  King  as  wishing  to  bring  down  the  prerogative  as
low  as  they  had  raised  him  on  high.  Of  this  and  further  statements
on  the  point  the  second  draft  does  not  contain  a  word.

The  differences  deserve  special  notice,  where  circumstances  con-
cerning the  clergy  are  discussed :  the  first  version,  according  to  my
conviction,  is  the  more  clear  and  energetic. Of  the  first  Convocation

74 DIFFERENCES  BETWEEN  BURNET 'S  MS.

it  is  said,  that  the  object  in  forming  a  commission  of  various -bishops
and  divines  for  altering  the  liturgy  was  this,  to  lay  a  scheme  before
Convocation,  whose  liberty  would  not  be  infringed  thereby.  In  the
second  elaboration  this  reservation  of  the  liberty  of  Convocation  is  not
mentioned  any  more.  In  the  first,  Lord  Clarendon  and  the  University
of  Oxford  appear  as  especially  hostile ;  this  is  not  the  case  in  the
second,  where  chief  stress  is  laid  on  the  unjustifiable  hostility  of  Con-
vocation. The  members  appear  in  the  first  as  instruments  of  a  party
which  is  bent  on  overthrowing  the  government ;  moreover  it  is  more
clearly  manifest  what  the  ground  of  the  opposition  was,  viz.,  that
further  alterations  would  lessen  the  dignity  of  the  Church.  The  printed
text  inserts  the  brief  remark,  that  the  bishops  had  not  sufficient
authority  to  rule  Convocation.  In  the  first  draft  it  is  said,  that  Con-
vocation had  not  met  again  since  then,  in  the  last,  that  it  did  not  meet
again  for  ten  years.  If  we  are  not  deceived,  we  can  from  this  last
divergence  draw  conclusions  as  to  the  origin  of  the  earlier.  The
second  draft  can  have  been  undertaken  at  the  earliest  in  the  year  1701,
in  which  Convocation  again  assembled,  that  is  after  ten  years,  and
perhaps  even  later,  in  times  in  which  the  strife  of  parties  had  fully
developed,  and  the  ill-will  between]  bishops  and  Convocation  had  ac-
quired political  significance.  In  the  second  draft  the  mention  of  the
favour  shown  to  Presbyterianism  in  Scotland  is  also  omitted,  although
this  is  of  essential  importance.

Enough ;  the  first  draft  contains  certain  facts,  which  are  omitted
in  the  second ;  possibly  not  because  they  were  found  to  be  incorrect,
but  because  they  no  longer  agreed  with  the  views  and  objects  of
the  later  time.

So  the  history  of  the  Corporations'  Bill,  by  means  of  which  the
Whigs  endeavoured  to  secure  the  upper  hand  for  ever,  is  told  in
the  first  draft  much  more  to  the  disadvantage  of  the  Whigs;  we
read  of  the  King's  anxiety,  lest  the  Whigs  should  be  willing  to
support  him  only  according  to  their  own  '  passions  and  humours.'  In
the  second  draft  this  is  omitted;  the  first  is  manifestly  both  more
impartial  and  more  instructive.

While  it  says  in  the  first  draft,  that  the  King  placed  the  military
forces  of  the  capital  in  the  hands  of  "the  Whigs,  in  the  other  one
reads  in  softened  phrase,  that  he  excluded  the  Tories  from  it ;  on
the  other  hand  the  claim  of  the  Tories,  which  at  first  appears  very  mild,
is  afterwards  expressed  in  stronger  and  condemnatory  words.  A
propos  of  the  confirmation  of  the  Acts  of  the  Convention  by  the
first  regularly  summoned  Parliament,  Burnet  had  remarked  in  his  first
draft,  that  it  had  been  brought  about  by  the  leaders  of  the  Tory  party,
who  made  use  of  their  followers  for  this  purpose,  before  they  had

AND  PRINTED  TEXT.  75

thought  much  about  it,  for  their  intention  had  been  to  give  the
King  a  proof  of  their  fidelity1;  in  the  later  one  this  is  omitted,
for  the  honour  then  is  not  to  be  allowed  to  the  Tories  of  having
contributed  to  the  establishment  of  the  new  order  of  things.  Another
and  less  honourable  rationale  of  their  conduct  is  inserted  instead.

It  is  undeniable,  that  the  second  draft  has  been  executed  with
very  deliberate  ill-will  against  the  Tories  and  against  the  tendencies
of  the  Episcopal  Church.  This  appears  very  surprisingly  in  the
descriptions  of  certain  leading  personages.

People  have  always  wondered,  that  the  Duke  of  Marlborough,
on  whose  personal  conduct  frequent  censures  have  been  passed
by  others,  has  been  so  very  kindly  treated  by  Burnet.  In  him
one  finds  nothing  either  of  the  equivocal  origin  of  the  Duke's
relation  to  James  II,  nor  yet  of  the  charge  brought  against  him
by  every  one  of  avariciousness.  In  the  first  draft,  however,  mention
was  made  of  both.  There  it  is  said  of  him  that  he  was  '  very  fit
for  business,  if  his  own  interests  prevailed  not  too  much  over  him  V
Burnet  here  adds  a  very  definite  accusation,  which  bears  the  stamp
of.  truth  on  it.  He  remarks  that  Churchill  (Marlborough)  never
shared  the  views  of  James  II,  gave  moderate  advice,  and  kept  aloof
from  his  council,  i.e.  his  camarilla;  but  he  was  content  to  make
use  of  his  post  in  the  army,  where  he  made  great  gains ;  for  money,
says  Burnet,  had  as  much  power  over  him  as  he  over  James  II.
Then  the  relation  of  his  sister  also  to  this  Prince  is  mentioned,
with  a  certain  reserve  no  doubt,  but  yet  without  concealment.  'Which
kindness/  he  says  of  James  IPs  favour  to  Marlborough,  '  had  begun
upon  the  King's  commerce  with  his  sister.'  All  this  appeared  there-
fore in  the  first  draft,  but  has  been  struck  out  in  the  second.  One
is  involuntarily  reminded  of  a  statement  originating  with  Lord
Dartmouth,  and  by  him  noted  as  trustworthy,  that  the  editor  of  the
History,  Thomas  Burnet,  son  of  Gilbert,  laid  the  MS.  first  before
the  Duchess  of  Marlborough,  and  altered  it  as  she  wished.  And
may  not  this  be  to  some  extent  true  ?  Certainly  one  must  assume
a  considerable  victory  over  self  on  her  part,  which,  however,  is  not
impossible,  if  one  is  to  suppose  that  she  sanctioned  all  that  is  there
said  about  herself.  She  appears  as  violent  and  rash  in  her  resolves,
proud  of  the  favour  which  she  enjoys,  and  even  insolent. In  this

description  of  the  Duchess  the  author  has  omitted  in  the.  second
draft  something  that  he  had  said  in  the  first,  viz.,  that  she  had  ruled
the  thoughts  and  inclinations  of  her  mistress,  the  Princess  Anne.
But  he  could  not  himself  have  wished  to  say  this  any  longer  at  a
time  in  which  the  influence  of  the  Duchess,  after  the  accession  of
the  Princess,  determined  the  direction  of  the  whole  state.  And  this
is  not  the  only  passage  in  which  party  spirit  appears.  In  the  course
of  the  History  Marlborough,  his  policy,  and  his  transactions  are
spoken  of  times  without  number;  of  the  ultimate  objects  of  his
ambition,  the  prosecution  of  which  in  fact  caused  his  overthrow,  one
learns  nothing  whatever.

While  Marlborough,  the  leader  of  the  Whigs,  is  treated  much
more  kindly  in  the  second  draft  than  in  the  first,  the  opposite  is
the  case  with  the  leader  of  the  Tories  and  of  the  Church  party,
Lord  Nottingham.  In  the  first  he  is  highly  praised,  as  the  best  son,
the  best  brother,  that  Burnet  had  ever  known,  as  a  man  of  exemplary
life,  and  as  a  good  lawyer  and  orator,  who  had  a  noble  style  of
expressing  himself,  but  was  a  little  too  lengthy  and  elaborate,  had
too  lofty  a  notion  of  the  prerogative  and  was  too  bitter  against  the
Whigs,  but  yet  was  far  removed  from  personal  aims  and  passions.
In  the  second  draft  all  this  retires  far  into  the  background.  His
manner  of  speaking  is  characterised  as  too  florid  and  therefore
tedious;  it  pleased  no  one  but  the  orator  himself  and  those  who
did  not  know  him.  Instead  of  the  words  of  the  first  draft  'he  is
learned  in  the  law/  one  reads  in  the  second  '  he  had  some  knowledge
of  the  law.'  The  '  learning '  here  degenerates  into  '  some  know-
ledge.' Still  more  strongly  does  this  difference  manifest  itself
in  those  places,  in  which  Burnet  speaks  of  the  activity  of  Nottingham
as  a  statesman.  In  the  printed  text  his  nomination  to  the  post  of
Secretary  of  State  appears  almost  as  a  mistake  of  the  King's ;  it
pleased  some,  but  excited  jealousy  in  others.  How  utterly  different
from  the  first  draft !  Nottingham  appears  in  that  as  a  joint-founder
of  the  new  order  of  things,  who  persuaded  his  friends  and  the  supporters
of  the  Church  to  take  the  oath  of  allegiance  to  the  government.
It  is  clear  at  the  first  glance,  what  a  great  service  he  thereby  did
King  William,  who  in  fact  found  his  chief  obstacle  in  ecclesiastical
antipathies.  In  the  midst  of  his  protestations,  that  he  intends  to
say  nothing  but  what  is  historical,  Burnet  breaks  out  with  the  words, —
Nottingham  saved  first  the  Church  and  then  the  state.  Thus  wrote
Burnet  at  a  time,  when  the  opposition  between  the  two  parties  had
not  yet  swallowed  up  everything,  when  he  himself,  as  also  even  the
King,  held  aloof  between  Whigs  and  Tories.  Later  on  he  went
over  to  the  Whigs;  but  it  must  always  surprise  us  that  he  should
then  have  so  completely  transformed  his  earlier  view.

AND  PRINTED  TEXT.  77

Burnet  has  here  and  there  made  corrections  in  style,  especially
in  sketching  persons'  characters ;  but  these  lie  outside  our  province  :
the  alterations  in  the  text  which  we  are  considering  are  not  matters
of  style,  but  of  politics ;  still  they  have  a  literary  side  also.

The  instances  quoted  are  enough  to  show,  that  the  author's
narrative  has  not  gained  by  them.  In  the  first  draft,  persons  and
events  appear  more  as  they  were.  The  notices,  which  he  afterwards
struck  out,  are  indispensable  to  a  historical  conception  of  the  first
ordering  of  the  state  under  William  III;  I  have  more  than  once
had  occasion  to  avail  myself  of  them ;  we  cannot  gain  a  true
idea  either  of  Marlborough  or  of  Nottingham,  unless  along  with
the  incomparable  talents  of  the  one  we  take  into  account  his  faults
also,  and  along  with  the  party  position  of  the  other  the  excellencies
also,  which  made  it  endurable.

Ought  not  the  natural  self-love  of  an  historical  writer  to  have  kept
the  author  from  ruining  his  own  work  ?  Considered  from  this  side
also  the  alterations  are  perplexing.  And  then  there  are  still  more  of
this  kind,  which  go  even  far  beyond  those  quoted.

One  knows  the  gallery  of  character-portraits  from  the  times  of
the  Restoration,  with  which  the  second  book  of  Burnet's  History
opens ;  they  have  greatly  contributed  towards  the  conception  of
the  persons,  which  has  become  dominant.  They  are  not  a  little  dry
and  contain  more  blame  than  appreciation.  How  surprising  then
that  Burnet  had  originally  made  sketches,  which  have  internal  truth,
and  give  proof  of  his  power  of  comprehending  human  nature :  I
think  these  original  conceptions  of  such  value,  and  at  the  same  time
so  characteristic  of  the  author's  original  tendencies,  that  they  ought
to  be  cited  just  as  they  are.  I  only  regret,  that  I  had  not  them
before  me  sooner.  Scarcely  anywhere  else  is  there  anything  which
gives  so  much  light  both  as  to  the  King  and  still  more  as  to  the
Duke  of  York.  Clarendon  appears  worse  in  the  adopted  text  than
in  the  original ;  Shaftesbury  better ;  and  this  corresponded  with  the
later  relations  of  the  Whigs.

Setting  aside  certain  weaknesses,  Burnet  appears  in  his  whole  life
as  a  worthy  prelate  and  a  well-meaning  man.  Could  the  spirit  of
party  have  become  so  completely  master  of  him  as  to  cause  him  to
make  the  alterations,  which  lie  before  us  ?  One  can  scarcely  suppose
it.  Is  not  the  later  editor  rather  to  blame?  And  if  so,  was  it
external  influence  or  his  own  blindness  that  was  at  work,  or  both  ?

I  do  not  venture  to  decide  these  questions.  But  it  is  manifest,
that  the  original  view  deserves  to  be  given  unaltered  to  the  historical
public.

7S DIFFERENCES  BETWEEN  BURNET'S  IMS.

Original  Sketches  of  Character  from  the  Manuscript.
(British  Museum. Harley,  6484).

i.  King  Charles  II.

The  King  is  certainly  the  best  bred  man  in  the  world,  for  the
Queen  mother  observed  often  the  great  defects  of  the  late  King's
breeding  and  the  stiff  roughness  that  was  in  him,  by  which  he  dis-
obliged very  many  and  did  often  prejudice  his.  affairs  very  much ;  so
she  gave  strict  orders  that  the  young  princes  should  be  bred  to  a
wonderfull  civility.  The  King  is  civil  rather  to  an  excess  and  has  a
softeness  and  gentleness  with  him,  both  in  his  air  and  expressions  that
has  a  charm  in  it.  The  Duke  would  also  pass  for  an  extraordinary
civil  and  sweet  tempered  man,  if  the  King  were  not  much  above  him
in  hit,  who  is  more  naturally  and  universally  civil  than  the  Duke.
The  King  has  a  vast  deal  of  wit,  indeed  no  man  has  more,  and  a  great
deal  of  judgement,  when  he  thinks  fitt  to  employ  it ;  he  has  strange
command  of  himselfe,  he  can  pass  from  business  to  pleasure  and  from
pleasure  to  business  in  so  easy  a  manner  that  all  things  seem  alike  to
him ;  he  has  the  greatest  art  of  concealing  himselfe  of  any  man  alive,
so  that  those  about  him  cannot  tell,  when  he  is  ill  or  well  pleased,  and
in  private  discourse  he  will  hear  all  sorts  of  things  in  such  a  manner,
that  a  man  cannot  know,  whether  he  hears  them  or  not,  or  whether
he  is  well  or  ill  pleased  with  them.  He  is  very  affable  not  only  in
publick  but  in  private,  only  he  talks  too  much  and  runns  out  too  long
and  too  farr ;  he  has  a  very  ill  opinion  both  of  men  and  of  women,
and  so  is  infinitely  distrustfull,  he  thinks  the  world  is  governed  wholly
by  interests,  and  indeed  he  has  known  so  much  of  the  baseness  of
mankind,  that  no  wonder  if  he  has  hard  thoughts  of  them ;  but  when
he  is  satisfied,  that  his  interests  become  likewise  the  interests  of  his
Ministers,  then  he  delivers  himself  up  to  them  in  all  their  humours
and  revenges  for  excusing  this.  He  has  often  said,  that  he  must
oblige  his  ministers  and  support  their  credit  as  necessary  for  his  ser-
vice, yet  he  has  often  kept  up  differences  amongst  his  ministers  and
has  ballanced  his  favours  pretty  equally  among  them,  which  consider-
ing his  tempers  must  be  uneasy  to  them,  except  it  be  that  there  is  art
necessary,  and  he  naturally  inclines  for  refineings  and  loves  an  in-
trigue. His  love  of  pleasure  and  his  vast  expence  with  his  women
together  with  the  great  influence  they  have  had  in  all  his  affaires  both
at  home  and  abroad  is  the  chief  load  that  will  lay  on  him ;  for  not
only  the  women  themselves  have  great  power,  but  his  court  is  full  of
pimps  and  bauds,  and  all  matters,  in  which  one  desires  to  succeed,
must  be  put  in  their  hands. He  has  very  mercyfull  inclinations,  when

AND  PRINTED  TEXT.  79

one  submitts  wholly  to  him,  but  is  severe  enough  to  those  that  oppose
him  and  speeks  of  all  people  with  a  sharpness,  that  is  not  suitable  to
the  greatness  of  a  Prince.  He  is  apt  to  believe  what  is  told  him,  so
that  the  first  impression  goes  deepest,  for  he  thinks  all  apologies  are
lies ;  he  has  knowledge  in  many  things  chiefly  in  all  navy  affaires,  even
in  the  architecture  of  shipps  he  judges  as  critically  as  any  of  the  trade
can  do  and  knows  the  smallest  things  belonging  to  it,  he  understands
much  natural  philosophy  and  is  a  good  chymist,  he  knows  many  me-
chanical things  and  the  inferiour  parts  of  the  mathematicks,  but  not
the  demonstrative.  He  is  very  little  conversant  in  books,  and  young
and  old  he  could  never  apply  himself  to  literature :  he  is  very  kind  to
those  he  loves,  but  never  thinks  of  doeing  any  thing  for  them,  so  that,
if  they  can  find  things  for  themselves,  he  will  easily  enough  grant
them,  but  he  never  setts  himself  to  find  out  any  thing  for  them,  and
I  never  heard  of  above  three  or  four  instances  of  any  places,  that  he
gave  of  his  own  motion,  so  that  those,  who  have  received  most  of  his
bounty,  think,  they  owe  the  thanks  more  to  his  instruments  than  to
himself;  he  never  enters  upon  business  with  any  himself,  but  if  his
ministers  can  once  draw  him  into  business,  they  may  hold  him  at  it
as  long  as  they  will.  He  loves  his  ease  so  much,  that  the  great  secret
of  all  his  ministers  is  to  find  out  his  temper  exactly  and  to  be  easy  to
him.  He  has  many  odd  opinions  about  religion  and  morality,  he
thinks  an  implicitness  in  Religion  is  necessaiy  for  the  safety  of  Go-
vernment and  he  looks  upon  all  inquisitiveness  into  those  things  as
mischievious  to  the  State ;  he  thinks  all  appetites  are  free  and  that  God
will  never  damn  a  man  for  allowing  himselfe  a  little  pleasure,  and  on
this  has  so  fixed  his  thoughts,  that  no  disorders  of  any  kind  have  ever
been  seen  to  give  him  any  trouble  when  they  were  over,  and  in  sick-
ness, except  his  ague  in  79,  he  seemed  to  have  no  concern  on  his
mind,  and  yet  I  believe  he  is  no  Atheist,  but  that  rather  he  has  formed
an  odd  idea  of  the  Goodness  of  God  in  his  mind;  he  thinks,  to  be
wicked  and  to  design  mischief,  is  the  only  thing  that  God  hates,  and
has  said  to  me  often,  that  he  was  sure,  he  was  not  guilty  of  that.  I
think  I  have  gone  pretty  far  and  scarce  know  how  I  should  scape
under  the  present  Chief  Justice,  if  this  should  happen  to  be  seased  on.

2.  The  Duke  of  York.

I  go  next  to  the  Duke ;  he  has  not  the  King's  witt  nor  quickness,
but  that  is  made  up  by  great  application  in  so  much,  that  he  keeps  a
journal  of  all  that  passes,  of  which  he  shewed  me  once  a  great  deal,
and  he  has  employed  the  late  Dutchesse  to  write  it  out  in  the  style  of
a  History,  for  she  writes  very  correctly,  and  he  intended  to  have  made

8o DIFFERENCES  BETWEEN  BURNET'S  MS.

me  prosecute  what  she  has  begun,  what  he  shewed  me.  He  has  natu-
rally a  candour  and  a  justice  in  his  temper  very  great,  and  is  a  firm
friend,  but  a  heavy  enemy  and  will  keep  things  long  in  his  mind  and
wrait  for  a  fitt  opportunity.  He  has  a  strange  notion  of  government,
that  every  thing  is  to  be  carried  on  in  a  high  way  and  that  no  regard
is  to  be  had  to  the  pleasing  the  people ;  he  has  an  ill  opinion  of  any
that  proposes  soft  methods  and  thinks  that  is  popularity,  but  at  the
same  time  he  always  talks  of  Law  and  Justice.  He  is  apt  enough  to
receive  an  enemy  upon  an  absolute  submission,  but  he  will  strain  hard
to  ruin  an  Enemy  that  stands  out,  and  when  I  knew  him  he  scorned
at  arts  to  take  them  off  (as  the  phrase  at  court  was  of  bringing  over
leading  men  in  the  house  of  Commons  to  their  party)  nor  will  he  re-
ceive any  upon  half  submissions,  and  he  thinks  that  all  who  oppose
the  King  in  parliament  are  rebells ;  he  understands  business  better
than  is  generally  believed,  for  tho'  he  is  not  a  man  of  witt  nor  fancy,
yet  he  generally  judges  well  when  things  are  laid  before  him,  except
when  the  violence  of  his  spirit  gives  him  a  byas,  which  it  does  too
often.  He  is  a  prince  of  great  courage  and  very  serious  in  action  and
naturally  hates  a  coward,  unless  it  be  to  make  use  of  him  in  the  con-
duct of  his  amours;  he  abhorrs  drunkenness,  he  never  swears  and
talks  irreligiously ;  he  has  pursued  many  secret  pleasures,  but  never
to  an  open  avowing  them,  and  he  does  condemn  himself  for  it,  but
yet  he  is  ever  going  from  one  intrigue  to  another,  tho'  it  is  generally
thought,  that  these  have  been  very  fatal  to  him  and  that  the  death  of
so  many  of  his  Children  is  owing  to  that.  He  is  a  zealous  and  hearty
papist,  of  which  he  gave  me  this  account :  when  he  was  in  Flanders
being  in  a  Nunnery,  a  Nunn  pressed  him  much  about  Religion  and
begged  him  to  use  this  prayer  every  day  to  God,  that  if  he  was  not  on
the  right  way  he  would  guide  him  to  it,  which  he  said  sunk  deep  in
his  mind  and  raised  scruples  in  him.  I  asked  him,  if  he  was  in  love
with  the  nun,  but  he  assured  me,  she  was  no  tempting  object.  He
was  reconciled  to  the  Church  of  Rome  while  he  was  in  Flanders,  but
he  dissembled  the  matter  long  after  that.  The  truth  was,  he  had
some  tinctures  in  his  education,  that  disposed  him  the  more  to  this,
he  was  bred  to  believe  a  mysterious  sort  of  reall  presence  in  the  Sa-
crament, so  that  he  thought  he  made  no  great  step,  when  he  believed
Transsubstantiation,  and  there  was  infused  in  him  very  early  a  great
reverence  for  the  Church  and  a  great  submission  to  it ;  this  was  done
on  design  to  possess  him  with  prejudices  against  presbytery,  for  that
was  the  thing  of  which  the  clergy  was  then  most  affraid,  but  it  has
this  ill  effect,  that  he  came  to  think,  that  if  a  church  was  to  be  sub-
mitted to,  it  was  more  reasonable  that  it  should  be  the  Church  of
Rome  than  the  Church  of  England. He  is  very  firm  in  his  per-

suasion,  but  he  has  not  inquired  much  into  it  and  is  very  much  de-
voted to  his  priests ;  yet  when  I  knew  him  he  seemed  very  positive  in
his  opinion  against  all  persecution  for  conscience'  sake,  but  I  look
on  that  only  as  a  thing  put  in  his  mouth  by  his  priests,  for  certainly
he  must  be  of  another  mind,  if  he  comes  to  have  power  in  his  hands ;
yet  I  have  wondered  much  at  one  thing,  that  being  so  firm,  as  he  is,
in  his  religion,  he  left  his  daughters  so  entirely  in  the  hands  of  the
divines  of  the  Church  of  England,  that  he  never  made  any  attempt  on
them  to  persuade  them  to  change,  of  what  the  Princess  of  Orange
assured  Dr.  Lloyd  who  waited  her  over  into  Holland.  It  is  very  hard

gion; he  had  indeed  an  answer  ready  to  another  thing,  which  I  tooke
the  freedom  to  object  to  him,  which  was,  that  the  rest  of  his  life  was
not  so  exact,  that  so  high  a  zeal,  as  he  has  shewed  in  his  Religion,
would  be  believed  to  flow  from  an  inward  sense  of  his  duty  to  God,
otherwise  that  would  appear  in  other  things ;  his  answer  was,  that  a
man  might  have  a  perswasion  of  his  duty  to  God  so  as  to  restrain
him  from  dissembling  with  God  and  man  in  professing  himselfe  to  be
of  another  Religion  than  that  which  he  believed  was  true,  tho'  it  did
not  yet  restrain  all  his  appetites.  He  was  so  far  from  being  displeased
with  me  for  taking  the  freedom  of  speaking  to  him  on  so  tender  a
point,  that  he  not  only  seemed  to  take  it  well,  but  he  has  spoken  very
kindly  of  me  to  many  others  upon  the  very  account.

3.  Monk.

As  for  Monck  he  deserves  not  a  character  so  much  for  his  own
merit,  as  for  the  luck  he  had,  to  be  so  great  an  instrument  in  the
bringing  home  the  King.  He  was  a  good  officer,  had  much  desperate
courage,  but  was  an  illiterate  and  injudicious  man,  and  was  neither  a
man  of  Religion  nor  strict  vertue ;  he  was  by  force  put  on  a  glorious
action  after  he  saw  there  was  nothing  else  to  be  done,  for  the  stream
ran  so  strong  for  bringing  home  the  King,  that  it  could  not  be  re-
sisted ;  so  Sir  Tho.  Clergis  and  his  wife  put  him  on  to  the  noble  reso-
lution, which  brought  so  much  wealth  and  honour  on  him,  whilst
alive,  and  has  left  so  much  fame  on  his  name.  The  King  carried
himself  always  with  great  respect  to  him,  but  he  had  no  value  for  him
in  his  heart.

4.  The  Earl  of  Clarendon.

The  great  man  with  the  King  was  Chancellor  Hyde,  afterwards
made  Earl  of  Clarendon.  He  had  been  in  the  beginning  of  the  long
Parliament  very  high  against  the  judges  upon  the  account  of  the  ship-
money  and  he  became  then  a  considerable  man. He  spoke  well,  his

sume and  dictate  too  much.  He  was  in  ill  terms  with  the  Duke  in
